docs.title: Emanate
docs.text:
Emanate is a unidirectional architecture for Kotlin where every behaviour of a screen is a small piece you can swap, intercept, reuse and test on its own.

You describe a screen with three plain types (a state, the actions of the user and the one-shot events) and an EmaViewModel that handles each action with middlewares, reducers and side effects. Emanate takes care of everything around them: lifecycle, coroutines, concurrency, navigation, process death, logs and errors.

Building block What it is You write State An immutable data class with everything the screen shows. data class HomeState(...) : EmaState Action Something the user did. sealed interface HomeAction : EmaAction Event Something that happened in the feature, delivered to the view once. sealed interface HomeEvent : EmaEvent

The view renders the state, reports what the user did with actions and reacts to events. It never holds business logic.

docs.title: A screen in a few lines
docs.text:
Each piece is declared for the type of action it handles. This home screen searches the friends of the user as they type:

class HomeViewModel(private val getFriendsUseCase: GetFriendsUseCase) :
    EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(HomeState()) {

    override fun setup() = source {
        middlewares {
            // Debounce: only the last query typed in 300 ms continues
            add<HomeAction.QueryWritten> { nextAfter(id = "search") { delay(300) } }
        }
        reducers {
            // The next state for every action of the screen
            add<HomeAction> { action ->
                when (action) {
                    is HomeAction.QueryWritten -> state.copy(query = action.query)
                    is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted -> state.copy(isLoading = true)
                    is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded -> state.copy(isLoading = false, friends = action.friends)
                    is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed -> state.copy(isLoading = false, dialog = HomeDialog.LoadError)
                    is HomeAction.FriendClicked -> state
                }
            }
        }
        sideEffects {
            // Searches with the new query, cancelling the previous search if it is still running
            add<HomeAction.QueryWritten>(concurrency = SideEffectConcurrency.Latest) {
                dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted)
                getFriendsUseCase(GetFriendsUseCase.Input(state.query))
                    .onSuccess { friends -> dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded(friends)) }
                    .onFailure { dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed) }
            }
            // Tells the view to open the profile
            add<HomeAction.FriendClicked> { action -> publish(HomeEvent.FriendSelected(action.friend)) }
        }
    }
}
  • The middleware waits until the user stops typing before the query continues.
  • The reducer returns the next state for each action, so the view always draws a valid state.
  • The side effects run the business logic and report it with actions (HomeAction.SideEffects) or events.

The same pieces can also be declared as properties of the ViewModel, with middlewareOf, reducerOf and sideEffectOf, and installed with add. Then each one can be reused, received in the constructor to change it by environment, or tested on its own:

class HomeViewModel(private val getFriendsUseCase: GetFriendsUseCase) :
    EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(HomeState()) {

    private val searchDebounce = middlewareOf(HomeAction.QueryWritten::class) {
        nextAfter(id = "search") { delay(300) }
    }

    private val homeReducer = reducerOf(HomeAction::class) { action ->
        when (action) {
            is HomeAction.QueryWritten -> state.copy(query = action.query)
            is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted -> state.copy(isLoading = true)
            is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded -> state.copy(isLoading = false, friends = action.friends)
            is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed -> state.copy(isLoading = false, dialog = HomeDialog.LoadError)
            is HomeAction.FriendClicked -> state
        }
    }

    private val searchFriends = sideEffectOf(HomeAction.QueryWritten::class, SideEffectConcurrency.Latest) {
        dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted)
        getFriendsUseCase(GetFriendsUseCase.Input(state.query))
            .onSuccess { friends -> dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded(friends)) }
            .onFailure { dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed) }
    }

    private val openFriend = sideEffectOf(HomeAction.FriendClicked::class) { action ->
        publish(HomeEvent.FriendSelected(action.friend))
    }

    override fun setup() = source {
        middlewares { add(searchDebounce) }
        reducers { add(homeReducer) }
        sideEffects {
            add(searchFriends, openFriend)
        }
    }
}

Start with Getting started, or see what these pieces make possible in Why Emanate.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text: Module Contents emanate-core Kotlin Multiplatform. All the code lives in commonMain. emanate-android Android integration: configuration, initializers, permissions and the saved state store. emanate-compose-android Compose support. It doesn't depend on any navigation library. emanate-compose-android-nav2 Navigation Compose support (emaScreen, emaDialog). emanate-serialization Kotlin Multiplatform. Saves serializable values of the state with kotlinx.serialization. emanate-test JVM utilities to test EmaViewModel and EmaSource, a friend module of emanate-core. sample A separate Gradle build with the sample app. It includes the library modules from the repository.

docs.title: Building
docs.text: ./gradlew assembleDebug

docs.title: The targets of emanate-core
docs.text:
emanate-core compiles its two kinds of targets, JVM (used by Android) and iOS, by default, which is needed to publish it but slow for daily work. Choose the targets with the emanate.targets property, in your local.properties (not versioned) or with -Pemanate.targets=...:

# local.properties
emanate.targets=jvm

The valid values are all, jvm and ios (iosArm64 and iosSimulatorArm64), separated by commas. The JVM target is always compiled, because the Android modules use it.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Module Tests Command emanate-core commonTest, run on every enabled target ./gradlew :emanate-core:allTests emanate-android Robolectric ./gradlew :emanate-android:testDebugUnitTest emanate-serialization JVM tests ./gradlew :emanate-serialization:jvmTest emanate-compose-android Compose UI tests on Robolectric ./gradlew :emanate-compose-android:testDebugUnitTest emanate-compose-android-nav2 Navigation tests on Robolectric ./gradlew :emanate-compose-android-nav2:testDebugUnitTest emanate-test JUnit ./gradlew :emanate-test:test

The resources that only the tests need live in src/test/res, so they are not published.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
Kover aggregates the coverage of the modules:

./gradlew koverHtmlReport

The report is written to build/reports/kover/html. koverXmlReport writes the XML version.

docs.title: Code format
docs.text:
The code is formatted with Spotless and ktlint. The rules are in the .editorconfig of the repository: Android Studio code style and lines of up to 120 characters.

./gradlew spotlessApply   # format
./gradlew spotlessCheck   # verify

Run them from the sample folder too, for the sample app. The commits that only format the code are listed in .git-blame-ignore-revs; enable it once with git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The documentation is the docs/ folder, plain Markdown that renders on GitHub. Every page is in English (page.md) and in Spanish (page.es.md): when you change one, update the other too. To preview it as a website with MkDocs, the Material theme and the language selector:

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
.venv/bin/mkdocs serve

The site has a version selector, built with mike: dev is the documentation of develop and every release has its own version, with latest pointing to the last one. They are published automatically (see below). mkdocs build --strict runs in the CI, so broken links fail the pull request.

docs.title: Continuous integration and releases
docs.text:
Every pull request to develop or master must pass the Spotless, Tests and Docs checks before it can be merged.

Releases follow git-flow and are automated with GitHub Actions:

  1. Run the Start release workflow from develop (optionally with the version; by default it is the current one without -SNAPSHOT). It creates release/X.Y.Z, a commit that removes -SNAPSHOT and a pull request to master.
  2. Fix whatever is needed in the release/X.Y.Z branch and merge the pull request with a merge commit, not squash.
  3. The Finish release workflow creates the tag and the GitHub release, asks JitPack to build it, publishes the documentation of the version and opens a pull request sync/X.Y.Z to develop that starts the next X.(Y+1).0-SNAPSHOT. Merge it with a merge commit too.

The workflows that open pull requests need a RELEASE_TOKEN secret: a personal access token with the repo and workflow scopes. With the default token GitHub does not run the CI on those pull requests.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Android minSdk 24 or higher.
  • The library is built with Java 21 and Kotlin 2.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Add the JitPack repository:

// settings.gradle.kts
dependencyResolutionManagement {
    repositories {
        google()
        mavenCentral()
        maven { url = uri("https://jitpack.io") }
    }
}

Add the dependencies:

val emanateVersion = "7.0.0"

dependencies {
    implementation("com.github.carmabs.ema:emanate-android:$emanateVersion")
    implementation("com.github.carmabs.ema:emanate-compose-android:$emanateVersion")
    // Only if your screens are in a Navigation Compose graph
    implementation("com.github.carmabs.ema:emanate-compose-android-nav2:$emanateVersion")
}

For a pure Kotlin module, like a presentation module with the ViewModels, add only the core, and emanate-test to test them:

dependencies {
    implementation("com.github.carmabs.ema:emanate-core:$emanateVersion")
    testImplementation("com.github.carmabs.ema:emanate-test:$emanateVersion")
}

emanate-core is a Kotlin Multiplatform library, so it can also be used from the commonMain of a multiplatform module.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text: Artifact Use it for emanate-core State, actions, events, ViewModels, EmaSource, plugins and use cases. Pure Kotlin Multiplatform. emanate-compose-android Jetpack Compose screens, back handling, dialogs, permissions and previews. It doesn't depend on any navigation library. emanate-compose-android-nav2 Emanate screens in a Navigation Compose graph (emaScreen, emaDialog). See Compose navigation. emanate-android The integration with the Android platform: configuration, initializers, permissions and the store of the saved state. emanate-serialization Saves any serializable value of the state across process death. Based on kotlinx.serialization. See the backup plugin. emanate-test Records and checks EmaViewModel and EmaSource in your unit tests. See Testing.

docs.title: Initialize Emanate
docs.text:
Call Emanate.init once, when the application starts and before any ViewModel is created:

class MyApplication : Application() {

    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        Emanate.init(EmaConfiguration.Android(debug = BuildConfig.DEBUG))
    }
}

Register the application in AndroidManifest.xml (android:name=".MyApplication"). With BuildConfig.DEBUG, debug builds log every action and fail at once with any exception, and release builds don't log and keep working. See Configuration.

docs.title: Your first screen
docs.text:
A screen is made of a state, the actions the user can perform, the events it can emit and a ViewModel that connects them. This is a counter.

data class CounterState(val count: Int = 0) : EmaState

sealed interface CounterAction : EmaAction {
    data object Increment : CounterAction
}

sealed interface CounterEvent : EmaEvent {
    data class LimitReached(val limit: Int) : CounterEvent
}

class CounterViewModel :
    EmaViewModel<CounterState, CounterAction, CounterEvent>(CounterState()) {

    override fun setup() = source {
        reducers {
            add<CounterAction> { action ->
                when (action) {
                    is CounterAction.Increment -> state.copy(count = state.count + 1)
                }
            }
        }
        sideEffects {
            add<CounterAction.Increment> {
                if (state.count == LIMIT) publish(CounterEvent.LimitReached(LIMIT))
            }
        }
    }

    private companion object {
        const val LIMIT = 10
    }
}
  • The reducer returns the next state for each action, and the view is notified.
  • The side effect runs after the reducer, with the new state, and publish sends a one-shot event to the view.
  • The ViewModel never touches platform classes, so it can be tested as plain Kotlin and shared between platforms.

docs.title: The screen
docs.text:
A Compose screen is described by an EmaScreenContent:

class CounterScreenContent : EmaScreenContent<CounterState, CounterAction> {

    @Composable
    override fun onState(
        state: CounterState,
        actions: EmaActionDispatcher<CounterAction>
    ) {
        Column {
            Text(text = state.count.toString())
            Button(onClick = { actions.dispatch(CounterAction.Increment) }) {
                Text(text = "+")
            }
        }
    }
}

And it is added to the navigation graph of an activity, where its events are handled:

class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContent {
            val navController = rememberNavController()
            NavHost(
                navController = navController,
                startDestination = CounterScreenContent::class.routeId
            ) {
                emaScreen(
                    screenContent = CounterScreenContent(),
                    viewModel = { CounterViewModel() },
                    onEvent = { event ->
                        when (event) {
                            is CounterEvent.LimitReached -> Toast.makeText(
                                this@MainActivity,
                                "Limit: ${event.limit}",
                                Toast.LENGTH_SHORT
                            ).show()
                        }
                    }
                )
            }
        }
    }
}

viewModel is a lambda that creates the ViewModel. Use your dependency injection framework there, or create it directly as above: see Dependency injection. onEvent receives every event of the screen, to show a message, as here, or to navigate. More in Compose screens.

docs.title: The preview
docs.text:
onState only draws the state it receives, so a preview is one call: write it inside the screen content, give it any state and an EmaActionDispatcher.EMPTY, which ignores the actions. No ViewModel, no fake data source:

class CounterScreenContent : EmaScreenContent<CounterState, CounterAction> {

    // onState, as above

    @Preview
    @Composable
    private fun PreviewCounter() {
        onState(state = CounterState(count = 7), actions = EmaActionDispatcher.EMPTY)
    }
}

The IDE creates the screen content to draw the preview, so keep its constructor without parameters. Add one preview per interesting state (empty, loading, an error dialog...) to see every case of the screen at once.

docs.title: What just happened
docs.text:
1. The user taps the button: the screen calls actions.dispatch(Increment).
  2. The reducer of the ViewModel computes the next state.
  3. The screen receives the new state and recomposes.
  4. On the tenth tap the side effect also publishes LimitReached, which the screen shows once and consumes.

Continue with Why Emanate to see what else the same pieces can do, or with Architecture.

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
Emanate does not force any project structure: you can put everything in a single module and call your classes whatever you want. This page collects the way the sample app is organised, and why. Take what is useful for you.

Where to start

If you are just trying Emanate, skip the modules and start with one. The three habits worth adopting from day one are organise by feature, use the same names everywhere and keep the ViewModel clean. Splitting into modules can wait until the app grows.

docs.title: Split the app into modules
docs.text:
A module is a part of the project that is compiled on its own and can only use what it declares as a dependency. That limit is exactly what we want: if a module cannot see something, nobody can use it there by mistake.

The sample has six modules:

Module What lives here Type Depends on app The Application, the dependency injection setup and the manifest. Android app Everything ui Screen contents, navigators, dialogs, theme and resources. Android library presentation, domain, android-utils, emanate-compose-android presentation State, actions, events, initializers and ViewModels. Pure Kotlin domain domain Models, use cases and repository interfaces. Pure Kotlin emanate-core data Repository implementations, network and storage. Android library domain, android-utils android-utils Android helpers shared by several modules, like reading and saving JSON in SharedPreferences. Android library domain

Read the arrows as "can see": ui can see presentation, but presentation cannot see ui. Three details:

  • app sees every module, because it creates all the pieces with the dependency injection.
  • api exposes a dependency to the modules above. presentation declares domain with api, and domain declares emanate-core with api. So ui can use the models of domain that appear in the state, and every module can use emanate-core. With implementation, a module keeps its dependencies to itself.
  • android-utils also depends on domain, to work with its models.

docs.title: api or implementation?
docs.text:
Both declare a dependency. The difference is who else can see it:

Declaration Who sees the dependency Use it when implementation Only the module that declares it. The dependency is an internal detail. This is the default. api The module and every module that depends on it. Its types appear in your public code: states, actions, function signatures or superclasses.

Imagine the state of a home screen that contains a list of users and the role of each one:

data class HomeState(val users: List<User>, val role: Role) : EmaState   // User and Role live in domain

presentation uses api for domain because User and Role are models of domain and appear in the state, so whoever draws it needs to know them. domain uses api for emanate-core because its use cases extend EmaUseCase. data, in contrast, uses implementation for domain: nobody above needs to see it through data.

Don't mark everything with api: the modules would see too much, and a change in one of them would recompile the others. And if ui uses the models of domain directly, also declare implementation project(':domain') in ui, so it does not depend on presentation keeping its api.

docs.title: Why presentation and domain are pure Kotlin
docs.text:
Pure Kotlin means the module has no Android in it: no Context, no View, no R.string. This has two benefits:

  • The compiler enforces the architecture. A ViewModel cannot use a Context or a resource by mistake, because the module does not have them. You don't need to remember a rule or catch it in a review.
  • It is ready for Kotlin Multiplatform. emanate-core is multiplatform, so presentation and domain can become multiplatform modules and share the ViewModels with other platforms.

As a bonus, their tests run in milliseconds on your computer, with no emulator (see Testing).

docs.title: What goes where?
docs.text:
When you are not sure where a class goes, ask yourself this:

If the class... It goes in Draws something or needs Android to work (a composable, a navigator, a Toast) ui Decides what the screen shows (state, actions, events, ViewModel) presentation Is a business concept or a use case (User, GetFriendsUseCase), or the interface of a repository (FriendsRepository) domain Implements those repository interfaces, talking to the REST API or the database (FriendsRepositoryImpl) data

domain says what data it needs (the interface), and data decides how to get it (the implementation).

docs.title: Organise by feature
docs.text:
Group the files by screen, not by type. Don't create a package states/ with every state of the app and another viewmodels/ with every ViewModel: when you change the Home screen you would have to jump through five packages.

Instead, each screen is one package in presentation and another one in ui, with the same name:

presentation/…/presentation/home/         ui/…/ui/home/
├── HomeState.kt                           ├── HomeScreenContent.kt
├── HomeAction.kt                          └── HomeNavigator.kt
├── HomeEvent.kt
├── HomeDialog.kt
├── HomeViewModel.kt
└── HomeInitializer.kt   (only if the screen receives data)

Everything about Home is in two folders with the same name. To delete the screen, you delete them.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
If every screen follows the same convention, you can open any of them and know where things are. Take the Home screen as an example:

Type Convention Example State <Screen>State HomeState Default state companion object { val DEFAULT } HomeState.DEFAULT Action <Screen>Action, named after what the user did QueryWritten, FriendClicked Event <Screen>Event, named after what happened FriendSelected, CloseClicked ViewModel <Screen>ViewModel HomeViewModel Dialogs in state <Screen>Dialog HomeDialog.LoadError Results of side effects <Screen>Action.SideEffects.<What> HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded Compose content <Screen>ScreenContent HomeScreenContent Initializer <Screen>Initializer HomeInitializer.HomeUser Preview Preview<What>, with the prefix so the previews are together PreviewAdmin, PreviewLoading

The two rows with a hint are the ones that most help to understand the code:

// Action: it says what the user DID, not what we want to happen
data class QueryWritten(val query: String) : HomeAction     // yes
data class SearchFriends(val query: String) : HomeAction    // no: it sounds like an order

// Event: it says what HAPPENED, and the navigator decides what to do with it
data class FriendSelected(val friend: Friend) : HomeEvent   // yes
data class GoToFriendDetail(val friend: Friend) : HomeEvent // no: the ViewModel should not know about navigation

docs.title: Create base classes
docs.text:
When every ViewModel needs the same thing, write it once.

Create a base ViewModel even if it is empty at the beginning. The classes of Emanate (EmaViewModel...) belong to the library: you cannot modify them. A base class of your own is the opposite: it is your code, and it is the one place where you can add something that must affect every screen of the app (a logger, an error handling...) the day you need it. Without it, you would have to edit every ViewModel one by one. With it, you change a single class and keep the control of the app.

// In `presentation`: all the ViewModels extend it
abstract class BaseViewModel<S : EmaState, A : EmaAction, E : EmaEvent>(initialDataState: S) :
    EmaViewModel<S, A, E>(initialDataState)

Not everything belongs in a base class

A base class is shared by all the ViewModels, so put in it only what all of them need. For behaviour that only some screens need, prefer a plugin or an extension function of the setup to a deeper hierarchy (BaseViewModel → BaseListViewModel → BasePaginatedListViewModel...). Creating subclasses of the base class is an anti-pattern: prefer composition over inheritance.

docs.title: Keep the ViewModel clean
docs.text: The ViewModel is the part of the app that is easiest to test, if you keep it simple. These rules protect that.

docs.title: No platform types
docs.text: A ViewModel must not use a context, a view or resources.

docs.title: Each piece has a single job
docs.text:
• Repositories are only used from use cases, never from a ViewModel directly.

    // Bad: the ViewModel talks to the repository
add<HomeAction.RefreshRequested> { repository.getFriends(state.query) }

// Good: it goes through a use case
add<HomeAction.RefreshRequested> { getFriendsUseCase(GetFriendsUseCase.Input(state.query)) }

  • Use cases do one thing, and receive a single Input data class, declared inside the use case itself, instead of several loose parameters.

    class GetFriendsUseCase(private val repository: FriendsRepository) :
    EmaUseCase<GetFriendsUseCase.Input, List<Friend>>() {

    override suspend fun useCaseFunction(input: Input): List<Friend> =
        repository.getFriends(input.query, input.onlyOnline)

    data class Input(val query: String, val onlyOnline: Boolean = false)
}

// In a side effect: each value is named, so the call explains itself
getFriendsUseCase(GetFriendsUseCase.Input(query = state.query, onlyOnline = true))

    The call reads clearly (onlyOnline = true instead of a lone true), and when the use case needs a new value you add a field with a default to Input, without changing the places that already call it. See Use cases for more.

  • Reducers only compute the state. The business logic (calls to the backend, saving...) goes in the side effects.

    Important: a reducer must be a pure, idempotent function

    Given the same state and the same action, it must always return the same new state, and do nothing else: no calls to the backend, no reading the clock or random numbers, no changing anything outside the state. That makes the state predictable and a reducer trivial to test. See Reducers.

    // Bad: the reducer calls the backend, and its result changes between calls
add<LoginAction.LoginClicked> { state.copy(user = repository.login(state.name)) }

// Good: the reducer only changes the state, the side effect does the work
reducers    { add<LoginAction.LoginClicked> { state.copy(isLoading = true) } }
sideEffects { add<LoginAction.LoginClicked> { dispatch(LoginAction.SideEffects.LoginResult(loginUseCase(...))) } }

docs.title: The view only reports and draws
docs.text:
• The view does not call ViewModel functions other than dispatch.
  • Put derived values in the state, not in the view, so the screen has no logic to test:
data class HomeState(val userData: UserData?, val userList: List<User>) : EmaState {
    val showCreateButton get() = userData?.role == Role.ADMIN   // the view only reads it
    val showEmptyList get() = userData != null && userList.isEmpty()
}

docs.title: Don't create your dependencies, receive them
docs.text:
A ViewModel often needs something that talks to the outside world: a use case that calls the backend, a database, the clock... Don't create it inside the ViewModel. Ask for it in the constructor and let someone else decide which one to give it.

// Bad: the ViewModel creates the real thing itself, so it always calls the real backend
class HomeViewModel : BaseViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(HomeState.DEFAULT) {
    private val getFriendsUseCase = GetFriendsUseCase(RemoteFriendsRepository())
}

// Good: it receives it, and does not know (or care) which one it is
class HomeViewModel(
    private val getFriendsUseCase: GetFriendsUseCase,
    initialState: HomeState
) : BaseViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(initialState)

The ViewModel is the same in both cases, but now whoever creates it chooses what it receives:

Where What it receives Why The app The real use case, which calls the backend. It is what the user needs. A unit test A fake that returns a fixed list. The test is fast and always gives the same result, with no network. A @Preview A fake with sample data. The preview draws without a backend. A QA build A fake that fails or is slow. You can see the error and loading states of the screen.

If the ViewModel created the use case itself, none of this would be possible without changing its code. See Dependency injection for how the sample does it with Koin.

It is not only for use cases. A ViewModel can also receive its middlewares, reducers and side effects, and then the injection decides how the whole screen behaves: for example, a side effect that returns fake friends in a QA build, or a middleware that adds latency to see the loading state. The ViewModel is written once and doesn't change. See Injecting pieces to learn how to write them, and Pieces are values to see how a piece is declared outside of setup.

docs.title: Strings
docs.text:
Provide the default language in values/ and the translations in values-xx/ (values-es/, values-fr/...). Keep the strings of every screen together and prefix them with the name of the screen, so you know where each one is used:

<string name="home_title">Friends</string>
<string name="home_empty_message">You have no friends yet</string>
<string name="login_error">Wrong user or password</string>

docs.title: Why Emanate
docs.text:
Most architectures tell you where to put your code. Emanate also changes what your code is made of.

In a classic ViewModel the behaviour of a screen is code inside its functions: to change it you edit the ViewModel, add an if or mock a whole repository. In Emanate every behaviour is a piece of code that reacts to an action, and every piece can be replaced:

Piece Runs Its job Middleware First, when an action arrives Decide the path of the action: let it continue, change it, delay it or stop it. Reducer Then, synchronously Return the next state. A pure function. Side effect After the reducers, asynchronously Run the business logic and report the result with actions or events. Broadcast Sent from a side effect Send an action to the other screens that listen to its type, like a result for the previous screen. Plugin Installed in the setup Group a set of pieces (middlewares, reducers, side effects) that work together, so they can be reused in different screens, like analytics or the backup of the state.

A piece can be a lambda written in the screen, a class, or an object received in the constructor. So the behaviour of a screen can be composed, replaced and inspected like any other data, and that unlocks things a classic architecture can't do without rewriting the screen.

docs.title: 1. Change how a screen behaves just by changing what you inject
docs.text:
The ViewModel receives the side effect that loads the friends of the user. Production injects the real one, the demo build a mock and the tests a fake. The ViewModel is the same in the three of them.

class HomeViewModel(private val loadFriends: FriendsEffect) :
    EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(HomeState()) {

    override fun setup() = source {
        reducers { /* ... */ }
        sideEffects {
            add(loadFriends)
        }
    }
}

// Production
HomeViewModel(LiveFriends(getFriendsUseCase))

// Demo build: no backend, a fixed list after half a second
HomeViewModel(MockFriends(friends = demoFriends))

Without Emanate the usual options are an if (isDemo) inside the ViewModel, a mocking library in the tests, or a fake repository for the whole app. Here you replace exactly the behaviour you want, and nothing else. See Dependency injection and environments.

docs.title: 2. Middlewares: step in before any action runs
docs.text:
A middleware sees every action of its type before the business logic and decides what happens to it, without the ViewModel knowing it. Inject them only where you need them:

// Two seconds of latency before every refresh, in the QA build
middlewareDelayOf<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeAction.RefreshRequested>(HomeAction.RefreshRequested::class, 2.seconds)

// Every refresh fails, to check the error dialog against the real backend
middlewareOf<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeAction.RefreshRequested>(HomeAction.RefreshRequested::class) {
    next(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed)
}

The same mechanism debounces a search field, stops the actions of a feature behind a flag or an expired session, replaces an action with another one, or tracks every action for analytics. Testing loading states and error dialogs no longer needs a broken network or a special backend. See Middlewares.

docs.title: 3. Plugins: write cross-cutting behaviour once and install it anywhere
docs.text:
A plugin is a reusable setup: it groups a set of middlewares, reducers and side effects that work together, and any screen installs it in one line. Analytics, logs, session checks, feature flags or the backup of the state are needed by many screens, so they are written once, as a plugin.

This one tracks every action of the screen and when the screen is shown:

class ScreenAnalytics<S : EmaState>(private val tracker: Tracker, private val screen: String) :
    EmaSourcePlugin<S, Nothing> {

    override fun install(setup: SourceSetupScope<S, Nothing, Nothing>) {
        // Sees every action of the screen before the reducers
        setup.middlewares {
            add<EmaAction> { action ->
                tracker.track(screen, action::class.simpleName.orEmpty())
                next()
            }
        }
        // Reacts to the lifecycle of the screen
        setup.sideEffects {
            add<EmaLifecycle.Resumed> { tracker.screenShown(screen) }
        }
    }
}

And any screen installs it:

override fun setup() = source {
    plugins {
        add(ScreenAnalytics<HomeState>(tracker, screen = "Home"))
    }
    reducers { /* ... */ }
}

No inheritance, no annotations and no code generation. See Plugins.

docs.title: 4. Concurrency under control
docs.text:
Each side effect has built-in mechanisms to manage the work queued for its actions: ignore new actions while one is running, cancel the running work when a new action arrives, or run them all in parallel, with timeouts and debounce. The classic bugs of a screen (the button tapped twice, the search that shows old results, the request triggered on every keystroke) are one parameter away:

sideEffects {
    // A second refresh while one is running is ignored
    add<HomeAction.RefreshRequested>(concurrency = SideEffectConcurrency.Leading) { /* ... */ }
    // A new query cancels the previous search
    add<HomeAction.QueryWritten>(concurrency = SideEffectConcurrency.Latest) { /* ... */ }
}
middlewares {
    // Debounce: only the last query of the last 300 ms continues
    add<HomeAction.QueryWritten> { nextAfter(id = "search") { delay(300) } }
}

See Side effects and Middlewares.

docs.title: 5. Results between screens, as typed actions
docs.text:
A screen can send a result to other screens by broadcasting an action. Every ViewModel that listens to its type receives it as one more action of its own, and handles it with its own reducers and side effects. No shared ViewModels, no result APIs of the platform and no casts:

// The profile screen broadcasts the friend it created
sideEffects {
    add<ProfileAction.SaveClicked> { broadcast(ProfileBroadcast.FriendCreated(state.friend), keepUntilReceived = true) }
}

// The home screen adds it to its list
override fun setup() = source {
    reducers {
        add<ProfileBroadcast.FriendCreated> { action -> state.copy(friends = state.friends + action.friend) }
    }
    broadcasts {
        listen<ProfileBroadcast.FriendCreated>()
    }
}

With keepUntilReceived, the result waits for the first screen that listens to it, even if that screen is not created yet. See Results between screens.

docs.title: 6. The whole history of a screen, with no extra code
docs.text:
Every action, state change, event and side effect goes through the same pipeline, so everything that happens on the screen is traced without writing a line for it. The testing module records that history in order, so a test checks the whole flow step by step, with virtual time:

val viewModel = HomeViewModel(MockFriends(friends = listOf(ana)))
val recorder = viewModel.record()

viewModel.dispatch(HomeAction.RefreshRequested)
viewModel.dispatch(HomeAction.FriendClicked(ana))
advanceUntilIdle()

recorder.assertState { it.friends == listOf(ana) }
recorder.assertEvents(HomeEvent.FriendSelected(ana))

assertSetup() even fails when a piece can never run, like the reducer of a result that the screen forgot to listen to. See Testing.

docs.title: 7. Survive process death declaratively
docs.text:
The system can kill your app while the user is in another one. A backup plugin saves the fields you choose and restores them when the screen comes back, with no platform code in the ViewModel:

plugins {
    add(backupOf(stateStore) {
        add("search", save = { query }, restore = { saved -> copy(query = saved) })
    })
}

See Surviving process death.

docs.title: 8. One policy for every error
docs.text: Every EmaViewModel logs each action it receives and the state before and after it. The errors of any middleware, reducer or side effect go through a single configurable error policy: fail at once while developing, report and keep working in production. A sideEffectListener measures every piece of business logic.

docs.title: 9. Multiplatform
docs.text: emanate-core is pure Kotlin Multiplatform, with no platform dependency. The same ViewModels run in your Android app, in your unit tests and on iOS, so the presentation layer can be shared between both.

docs.title: The rules that make it work
docs.text: Emanate stays predictable because it keeps a few rules: the state only changes in the reducers, the view only renders and reports, and anything that lasts belongs in the state while anything that happens once is an event. Read them in Architecture.

docs.title: Compose back handling
docs.text: The user can go back in two ways: pressing the back arrow drawn in your toolbar, or using the system back (the back button or gesture of the phone). By default the system back simply closes the screen. This page explains how to take control of it, for example to ask "Are you sure you want to leave?" before the screen disappears.

docs.title: The idea in one minute
docs.text:
On every change of the state, Emanate asks your screen content one question:

"If the user presses back right now, should I do something special?"

You answer by implementing onBack, which receives the current state and returns:

You return What happens when the user presses back An action Emanate blocks the default behavior and sends that action to the ViewModel. The ViewModel decides what to do. null Emanate does nothing and the system handles back as usual (closes the screen).

Since the base implementation returns null, a screen that does not override onBack behaves like any other Android screen. You only write it when you need something different.

override fun onBack(state: ProfileCreationState): ProfileCreationAction? =
    if (state.dialog == null) ProfileCreationAction.OnBack else null

Read it as: "if there is no dialog open, turn back into the action OnBack; otherwise, leave it to the system".

docs.title: What Emanate does for you
docs.text:
Behind the scenes, Emanate installs a single BackHandler (the standard Compose tool to intercept back) and calls your onBack each time the state changes:

val backAction = screenContent.onBack(state)
BackHandler(enabled = backAction != null) {
    backAction?.also(actions::dispatch)
}

So you never create a BackHandler yourself. You only decide, state by state, whether to intercept and with which action. Returning null in some states is how you switch the interception off.

Why it receives the state

Because onBack gets the state, the decision can depend on it. A form could intercept back only when there are unsaved changes, and let the user leave freely when everything is saved.

docs.title: Example 1: confirm before leaving
docs.text:
The profile creation screen has a form. If the user presses back, we don't want to lose what they typed by accident, so we show a confirmation dialog first.

The flow has four steps:

  1. The user presses back (the arrow or the system back).
  2. onBack returns OnBack, so Emanate sends that action to the ViewModel.
  3. The ViewModel puts the dialog in the state and the screen draws it.
  4. If the user confirms, the ViewModel publishes an event and the navigator closes the screen.

docs.title: Step 1: the screen content
docs.text:
Both ways of going back send the same action. The arrow does it in its onClick, and the system back does it through onBack:

class ProfileCreationScreenContent : EmaScreenContent<ProfileCreationState, ProfileCreationAction> {

    // System back
    override fun onBack(state: ProfileCreationState): ProfileCreationAction? =
        if (state.dialog == null) ProfileCreationAction.OnBack else null

    @Composable
    override fun onState(state: ProfileCreationState, actions: EmaActionDispatcher<ProfileCreationAction>) {
        // Back arrow of the toolbar
        IconButton(onClick = { actions.dispatch(ProfileCreationAction.OnBack) }) { /* arrow icon */ }

        // ... rest of the screen and the dialog
    }
}

docs.title: Step 2: the ViewModel
docs.text:
The ViewModel does not know (or care) whether the action came from the arrow or from the system back. It reacts to OnBack by opening the dialog, and to the confirmation by asking the navigator to leave:

reducers {
    add<ProfileCreationAction> { action ->
        when (action) {
            is ProfileCreationAction.OnBack -> state.copy(dialog = ProfileCreationDialog.BackConfirmation)
            is ProfileCreationAction.DialogBackConfirm -> state.copy(dialog = null)
            is ProfileCreationAction.DialogBackCancel -> state.copy(dialog = null)
            // ...
        }
    }
}
sideEffects {
    // The user confirmed: the navigator closes the screen
    add<ProfileCreationAction.DialogBackConfirm> { publish(ProfileCreationEvent.DialogConfirmationAccepted) }
}

docs.title: Step 3: the navigator closes the screen
docs.text:
The ViewModel cannot close a screen by itself: it publishes an event, and the code that registers the screen turns it into navigateBack(). See Navigation.

onEvent = { event ->
    when (event) {
        ProfileCreationEvent.DialogConfirmationAccepted -> navController.navigateBack()
    }
}

docs.title: Why return null while the dialog is open?
docs.text:
Look again at the condition: if (state.dialog == null) OnBack else null.

When the dialog is on screen and the user presses back, the dialog itself must handle it (usually by closing itself, which is what users expect). The dialogs drawn with AlertDialog or Dialog already do it, and they report it to you through onBackPressed in their listener, as explained in Dialogs.

If onBack kept returning OnBack with the dialog open, the screen would intercept back again and the ViewModel would open a second dialog over the first one. Returning null in that state avoids it.

State onBack returns Back press goes to No dialog OnBack The ViewModel, which opens the dialog Dialog open null The dialog, which closes itself

docs.title: Example 2: back that just goes back
docs.text:
Not every screen needs a confirmation. On the home screen, back simply returns to the login, like its close button. Even so, it is better to send an action than to leave the system do it, so there is a single path through the ViewModel for both the arrow and the system back:

// Screen content: the arrow and the system back send the same action
override fun onBack(state: HomeState) = HomeAction.CloseClicked

// ViewModel
sideEffects {
    add<HomeAction.CloseClicked> { publish(HomeEvent.CloseClicked) }
}

The navigator turns CloseClicked into navigateBack(). Having a single path has two advantages: you can add logic later (analytics, saving a draft...) in one place, and a test can check the behavior without drawing the screen: dispatch CloseClicked and assert the event.

docs.title: Which one do I need?
docs.text: I want... Do this Nothing special, the screen just closes Don't override onBack (it returns null) The ViewModel to know that the user left Return an action always, and publish the navigation event from the ViewModel To ask for confirmation before leaving Return the action only when there is something to protect, and show a dialog Back to work normally while a dialog is open Return null when the state has a dialog

docs.title: Compose dialogs
docs.text: A dialog is a small window that appears over the screen to tell something to the user or to ask a question: "Delete this note?", "The connection failed", "Discard your changes?". This page explains how to show one with Emanate, step by step, with a complete example you can copy.

docs.title: The idea in one minute
docs.text:
In Emanate a dialog is not something you open: it is something the state says. There is no dialog.show() and no dialog.dismiss(). Instead:

  1. The state has a field that says which dialog is open, or null if there is none.
  2. The screen draws the dialog while that field is not null.
  3. The buttons of the dialog don't close it. They send an action, and the ViewModel changes the field.

If you already know state, actions and reducers, there is nothing new here: a dialog is one more piece of the state.

Why do it this way?

  • It survives a rotation. The state is kept by the ViewModel, so the dialog is still there after the screen is recreated. A dialog opened with show() disappears.
  • The ViewModel knows what is on screen. It can decide things like "ignore this tap while a dialog is open".
  • You can test it without a device. The whole flow is state and actions: see Testing.

docs.title: Example: confirm before deleting a note
docs.text: We are going to build a screen with a Delete button. When the user presses it, a dialog asks for confirmation.

docs.title: Step 1: describe the dialogs in the state
docs.text:
Create a type that lists every dialog the screen can show. A sealed interface is perfect: each dialog is one case, and the compiler will warn you if you forget to draw one.

sealed interface NoteDialog {
    data object ConfirmDelete : NoteDialog
}

data class NoteState(
    val title: String = "",
    val dialog: NoteDialog? = null     // null = no dialog open
) : EmaState

dialog is nullable on purpose: null means "nothing is open".

docs.title: Step 2: describe what the user can do
docs.text:
Every button of the screen and of the dialog is an action:

sealed interface NoteAction : EmaAction {
    data object DeleteClicked : NoteAction          // the Delete button of the screen
    data object DeleteConfirmed : NoteAction        // "Accept" in the dialog
    data object DeleteCancelled : NoteAction        // "Cancel" in the dialog, or back, or tapping outside
}

sealed interface NoteEvent : EmaEvent {
    data object NoteDeleted : NoteEvent
}

docs.title: Step 3: the ViewModel opens and closes the dialog
docs.text:
Opening a dialog is writing it in the state. Closing it is writing null:

class NoteViewModel(private val deleteNote: DeleteNoteUseCase) :
    EmaViewModel<NoteState, NoteAction, NoteEvent>(NoteState()) {

    override fun setup() = source {
        reducers {
            add<NoteAction> { action ->
                when (action) {
                    is NoteAction.DeleteClicked -> state.copy(dialog = NoteDialog.ConfirmDelete)   // open
                    is NoteAction.DeleteCancelled -> state.copy(dialog = null)                     // close
                    is NoteAction.DeleteConfirmed -> state.copy(dialog = null)                     // close
                }
            }
        }
        sideEffects {
            // The work is done after confirming: the dialog is already closed
            add<NoteAction.DeleteConfirmed> {
                deleteNote(Unit)
                publish(NoteEvent.NoteDeleted)
            }
        }
    }
}

Notice that confirming does two things, and each one lives where it belongs: the reducer closes the dialog (it is state) and the side effect deletes the note (it is work). See reducers and side effects if you need a reminder.

docs.title: Step 4: the screen draws the dialog
docs.text:
In onState, check the field. If there is a dialog, emit the composable that draws it. Here we use the AlertDialog of Material 3, the standard dialog of Compose:

@Composable
override fun onState(state: NoteState, actions: EmaActionDispatcher<NoteAction>) {
    Column {
        Text(state.title)
        Button(onClick = { actions.dispatch(NoteAction.DeleteClicked) }) {
            Text("Delete")
        }
    }

    // The dialog is drawn only while the state says so
    when (state.dialog) {
        NoteDialog.ConfirmDelete -> AlertDialog(
            onDismissRequest = { actions.dispatch(NoteAction.DeleteCancelled) },   // back or tap outside
            title = { Text("Delete note") },
            text = { Text("This cannot be undone. Do you want to continue?") },
            confirmButton = {
                TextButton(onClick = { actions.dispatch(NoteAction.DeleteConfirmed) }) { Text("Delete") }
            },
            dismissButton = {
                TextButton(onClick = { actions.dispatch(NoteAction.DeleteCancelled) }) { Text("Cancel") }
            }
        )
        null -> Unit    // nothing to draw
    }
}

That is the whole feature. Let's follow what happens when the user presses Delete:

# What happens Who 1 The user presses the button. The screen sends DeleteClicked. Screen 2 The reducer returns state.copy(dialog = ConfirmDelete). ViewModel 3 The state changed, so onState runs again. Now state.dialog is not null, and the AlertDialog is drawn. Screen 4 The user presses Delete in the dialog. The screen sends DeleteConfirmed. Screen 5 The reducer returns dialog = null and the side effect deletes the note. onState runs again and the dialog is no longer drawn. ViewModel

The most common mistake

The onDismissRequest of AlertDialog is called when the user presses back or taps outside the dialog. It does not close it. If you leave it empty (onDismissRequest = {}), the dialog can never be dismissed that way, and if you try to hide it with a local var, the state and the screen get out of sync. Always dispatch an action that sets dialog = null.

docs.title: Dialogs that carry data
docs.text:
A dialog often needs information: which note is going to be deleted? Use a data class instead of a data object and put the data inside:

sealed interface NoteListDialog {
    data class ConfirmDelete(val noteId: Int, val noteTitle: String) : NoteListDialog
    data class Error(val message: EmaText) : NoteListDialog
}

// Reducer: the dialog is created with the data of the tapped note
is NoteListAction.DeleteClicked -> state.copy(
    dialog = NoteListDialog.ConfirmDelete(action.note.id, action.note.title)
)

// Screen: each case of the sealed type is drawn differently
when (val dialog = state.dialog) {
    is NoteListDialog.ConfirmDelete -> AlertDialog(
        onDismissRequest = { actions.dispatch(NoteListAction.DialogDismissed) },
        title = { Text("Delete \"${dialog.noteTitle}\"?") },
        confirmButton = {
            TextButton(onClick = { actions.dispatch(NoteListAction.DeleteConfirmed(dialog.noteId)) }) {
                Text("Delete")
            }
        },
        dismissButton = {
            TextButton(onClick = { actions.dispatch(NoteListAction.DialogDismissed) }) { Text("Cancel") }
        }
    )
    is NoteListDialog.Error -> AlertDialog(
        onDismissRequest = { actions.dispatch(NoteListAction.DialogDismissed) },
        text = { Text(dialog.message.stringResource()) },
        confirmButton = {
            TextButton(onClick = { actions.dispatch(NoteListAction.DialogDismissed) }) { Text("OK") }
        }
    )
    null -> Unit
}

Because when over a sealed interface must be exhaustive, adding a new dialog to the type makes the compiler point you to the place where you have to draw it.

Only one dialog at a time

A nullable field can hold a single dialog. That is almost always what you want, since two stacked dialogs are confusing. If you really need two at once, use two fields.

docs.title: Avoid repeating yourself: a reusable dialog
docs.text:
When several dialogs look the same (a title, a message, Accept and Cancel), don't write the AlertDialog over and over. Wrap it once in your own composable that receives the texts and two lambdas:

@Composable
fun ConfirmationDialog(
    title: String,
    message: String,
    onConfirm: () -> Unit,
    onCancel: () -> Unit
) {
    AlertDialog(
        onDismissRequest = onCancel,
        title = { Text(title) },
        text = { Text(message) },
        confirmButton = { TextButton(onClick = onConfirm) { Text("Accept") } },
        dismissButton = { TextButton(onClick = onCancel) { Text("Cancel") } }
    )
}

// Use
NoteDialog.ConfirmDelete -> ConfirmationDialog(
    title = "Delete note",
    message = "This cannot be undone.",
    onConfirm = { actions.dispatch(NoteAction.DeleteConfirmed) },
    onCancel = { actions.dispatch(NoteAction.DeleteCancelled) }
)

docs.title: The dialog and the back button
docs.text:
While a dialog is on screen, the dialog must handle the back button, not the screen behind it. Make onBack return null when state.dialog is not null:

override fun onBack(state: NoteState): NoteAction? =
    if (state.dialog == null) NoteAction.BackClicked else null

If you forget it, the screen intercepts back and the dialog does too, and the user may see two dialogs one over the other. The full explanation is in Back handling.

docs.title: Loading: it is not always a dialog
docs.text:
A spinner is not necessarily a dialog. In most cases it is better to model it as a boolean of the state and draw a progress indicator where it belongs, for example inside the button that started the work:

data class LoginState(val isLoading: Boolean = false /* ... */) : EmaState

// Reducer
is LoginAction.LoginClicked -> state.copy(isLoading = true)
is LoginAction.LoginFinished -> state.copy(isLoading = false)

Button(onClick = { actions.dispatch(LoginAction.LoginClicked) }, enabled = !state.isLoading) {
    if (state.isLoading) CircularProgressIndicator(Modifier.size(18.dp)) else Text("Log in")
}

Use a blocking loading dialog only when the user must not touch anything while the work runs. Even then it is the same pattern: isLoading in the state, and if (state.isLoading) LoadingDialog() in the screen.

docs.title: Testing a dialog
docs.text:
Since the dialog is state and the choices are actions, you test the whole flow without drawing anything: dispatch the action, check the state.

@Test
fun `pressing delete asks for confirmation and confirming deletes the note`() = runTest {
    val viewModel = NoteViewModel(FakeDeleteNoteUseCase())
    val recorder = viewModel.record()

    viewModel.dispatch(NoteAction.DeleteClicked)
    recorder.assertState { it.dialog == NoteDialog.ConfirmDelete }

    viewModel.dispatch(NoteAction.DeleteConfirmed)
    advanceUntilIdle()

    recorder.assertState { it.dialog == null }
    recorder.assertEvents(NoteEvent.NoteDeleted)
}

See Testing for how to set up useTestConfiguration().

docs.title: Compose navigation
docs.text:
This page is about Navigation Compose, and it needs the emanate-compose-android-nav2 artifact. The rest of the Compose artifacts don't depend on any navigation library, so a different navigation can be used with EmaScreen.

In Emanate a ViewModel never navigates. Navigating is the job of the navigation graph that contains the screen, usually the NavHost: it is the one that knows which screens exist and holds the NavController to move between them.

The ViewModel only publishes an event that says what happened, like "the login succeeded". Someone outside the screens has to receive those events and decide where to go: the navigator, a class that lives next to the NavHost and holds its NavController. It is not a class of Emanate: it is a plain class of yours, and it is a good pattern to handle all the navigation of your app this way.

This is the main flow of the sample, with two of its screens, the login and the home:

  1. Each destination of the NavHost is an emaScreen, with its screen content, its ViewModel and its onEvent.
  2. When the credentials are right, the ViewModel of Login publishes LoginSuccess(user). It doesn't know which screen comes next.
  3. The onEvent of that screen hands the event to the navigator, to its function for that screen: handleLoginEvent.
  4. The navigator decides for each event: LoginSuccess opens Home, and the CloseClicked of Home goes back to the login. It does it with the navController, which changes the destination shown by the NavHost.

Keeping the navigation out of the ViewModel has two advantages. The ViewModel can be tested without Android, and the same event can lead to different places in different apps or graphs: on a phone it may open a new screen and on a tablet update a side panel.

The decision of where to go could be written directly in each onEvent lambda, but we recommend that every navigation goes through a navigator: the graph only declares the screens, and all the navigation of a flow lives in one place that is easy to read and to change. See The navigator.

docs.title: Routes
docs.text:
Every screen registered with emaScreen or emaDialog has a route. By default it is ScreenContent::class.routeId, unique per class:

navController.navigate(HomeScreenContent::class.routeId)

docs.title: The navigator
docs.text:
Create one navigator per navigation graph, not one per screen, and let it handle the navigation of all the screens of the graph. It is a plain class that receives the NavController and has one function per screen: each function receives the events of that screen and decides where to go. Emanate doesn't require a base class or an interface for it: any class with this shape works. Create it once, with remember, next to the NavHost:

class MainNavigator(private val navController: NavController, private val context: Context) {

    fun handleLoginEvent(event: LoginEvent, onMessage: (LoginEvent) -> Unit) {
        when (event) {
            is LoginEvent.LoginSuccess -> navController.navigate(
                route = HomeScreenContent::class.routeId,
                initializerBundle = EmaInitializerBundle(
                    HomeInitializer.HomeUser(event.user),
                    BundleSerializerStrategy.kSerialization(HomeInitializer.serializer())
                )
            )

            // A message is not navigation: whoever shows messages handles it
            is LoginEvent.Message -> onMessage(event)
        }
    }

    fun handleHomeEvent(event: HomeEvent, onMessage: (HomeEvent) -> Unit) {
        when (event) {
            // The profile creation is in its own activity
            HomeEvent.CreateClicked -> context.startActivity(Intent(context, ProfileActivity::class.java))

            // The login is the screen below the home
            HomeEvent.CloseClicked -> navController.navigateBack()

            is HomeEvent.UserCreated -> onMessage(event)
        }
    }
}

setContent {
    val navController = rememberNavController()
    val navigator = remember { MainNavigator(navController, context) }

    NavHost(navController, startDestination = LoginScreenContent::class.routeId) {
        emaScreen(
            screenContent = LoginScreenContent(),
            viewModel = { get<LoginViewModel>() },
            onEvent = { navigator.handleLoginEvent(it) { /* show the message */ } }
        )
    }
}

NavController.navigateBack(closeActivityWhenBackstackIsEmpty = true) pops the back stack and closes the activity when there is nothing left, and NavController.navigateToExternalLink(url) opens a link in another app.

docs.title: Passing an initializer
docs.text:
Send the initializer with the navigate extension that receives an EmaInitializerBundle:

navController.navigate(
    route = HomeScreenContent::class.routeId,
    initializerBundle = EmaInitializerBundle(
        HomeInitializer.HomeUser(user),
        BundleSerializerStrategy.kSerialization(HomeInitializer.serializer())
    )
)

Another overload receives a NavOptionsBuilder lambda, like navigate(route) { launchSingleTop = true }.

The destination declares where to read it from with initializerSupport. The initializer travels in the route as text, so Compose navigation reads it with kotlinx.serialization: the parcelable and serializable strategies, which only work with Bundles, can't be used in a route.

emaScreen(
    screenContent = HomeScreenContent(),
    viewModel = { get<HomeViewModel>() },
    initializerSupport = EmaInitializerSupport.fromRoute(HomeInitializer.serializer()),
    onEvent = { navigator.handleHomeEvent(it) { /* show the message */ } }
)

The initializer reaches the ViewModel as an action, the first time the screen is created. See Initializers.

docs.title: Where the initializer comes from
docs.text:
EmaInitializerSupport has one function per origin. The name says where the initializer is read from:

Function Where it reads the initializer When to use it fromRoute(serializer) The route of the destination. Most screens: the ones you reach with navigate(route, initializerBundle). fromIntent(serializer) The route and, if it has none, the intent of the activity. The first screen of an activity that is opened with an initializer. fromBundle(serializer, bundle) The route and, if it has none, the Bundle that you give it. A graph that receives its arguments in a Bundle. fromInitializer(serializer, initializer) The route and, if it has none, the initializer that you give it. An initializer that you already have, like the one of a deep link, or a test.

In all of them the route wins: if it carries an initializer, the screen uses it. The origin of the function is only the backup for when the route has none.

docs.title: The first screen of an activity
docs.text:
The initializer of a screen normally travels in its route: the navigator puts it there with navigate(route, initializerBundle), and fromRoute reads it back. But the first screen of a NavHost, its startDestination, is not reached with navigate: it is shown as soon as the NavHost is created, so its route has no initializer.

If that screen needs one, it can come from the intent of the activity. The sample doesn't need it, because the profile creation has no data to receive, but imagine that the home screen starts ProfileActivity and puts a ProfileCreationInitializer.Default("Carlos") in the intent, so that the creation screen can say who creates the user. It takes two steps, one in each activity:

1. Put the initializer in the intent of the activity that opens the graph. Use setInitializer of the Intent, with the serializer of the initializer, and start the activity:

val intent = Intent(context, ProfileActivity::class.java).setInitializer(
    ProfileCreationInitializer.Default("Carlos"),
    BundleSerializerStrategy.kSerialization(ProfileCreationInitializer.serializer())
)
context.startActivity(intent)

The initializer travels in the extras of the intent, under the key that Emanate reads. If you open the activity with a navigation graph of Android, as the sample does with an action that goes to an activity, navController.navigate(id, EmaInitializerBundle(...)) puts it there for you, and you only have to use the same serializer when you read it.

2. Declare the first screen with fromIntent. It reads the initializer from the intent of the activity that contains the NavHost, using the same serializer:

NavHost(navController, startDestination = ProfileCreationScreenContent::class.routeId) {
    emaScreen(
        screenContent = ProfileCreationScreenContent(),
        viewModel = { get<ProfileCreationViewModel>() },
        // The initializer that the home screen put in the intent of the activity
        initializerSupport = EmaInitializerSupport.fromIntent(ProfileCreationInitializer.serializer()),
        onEvent = { navigator.handleProfileCreationEvent(it) }
    )
}

You don't have to read the intent yourself. The rest of the screens of the graph are declared with fromRoute, so they never read the intent.

docs.title: When the first screen is opened again
docs.text:
The intent is a backup: the route wins. If the first screen is opened again later with navigate, it receives:

How it is opened The screen receives navigate(route, EmaInitializerBundle(Default("Ana"), ...)) Default("Ana"), the one of the route. navigate(route), without initializer Default("Carlos"), the one of the intent, as the first time. navigate(route, EmaInitializerBundle(Default(""), ...)) Default(""), the one of the route.

The last row is the way to avoid the backup. If the new screen must not use the initializer of the intent, navigate with an initializer of the screen without values, so that the route has one and wins. It is a normal initializer, of the type that the screen expects, with empty values:

navController.navigate(
    route = ProfileCreationScreenContent::class.routeId,
    initializerBundle = EmaInitializerBundle(
        ProfileCreationInitializer.Default(admin = ""),
        BundleSerializerStrategy.kSerialization(ProfileCreationInitializer.serializer())
    )
)

The screen then receives that initializer, and it is the reducer of ProfileCreationInitializer that decides what it means: for example, that there is no creator to show.

Going back to the first screen with the back button doesn't open it again: the original screen, with its ViewModel, comes back and doesn't read the initializer again.

docs.title: Permissions (Android)
docs.text: Some things an app wants to do are protected by Android: using the camera, reading the location, sending notifications... Before the app can do them, the user must say yes in a system dialog. This page explains how to ask for those permissions with Emanate, step by step, with a complete example you can copy.

docs.title: The idea in one minute
docs.text:
Asking for a permission is awkward for a ViewModel, because the system dialog belongs to the screen (the Activity), and the ViewModel must not know anything about Android. Emanate solves it with the same recipe as everything else:

  1. The ViewModel writes in the state that a permission is needed (requestingPermission = true).
  2. The screen sees it, asks Android for the permission, and waits for the user.
  3. When the user answers, the screen sends the answer as an action (PermissionAnswered), and the ViewModel decides what to do next.

The tool that talks to Android is EmaPermissionManager. It turns the system flow (launchers, callbacks...) into simple suspend functions.

docs.title: 1. Declare the permission in the manifest
docs.text:
Android ignores any permission that is not declared in AndroidManifest.xml, so this is the first thing to do:

<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.CAMERA" />

docs.title: 2. Know the three answers
docs.text:
When you ask, the result is a PermissionState:

PermissionState What it means Typical reaction GRANTED The user said yes (or had already said it). Do the thing that needed the permission. NOT_GRANTED The permission is not granted. Do without it, or tell the user it is needed. NOT_GRANTED_SHOULD_EXPLAIN Not granted, and the user already refused it once. Android recommends explaining why the app needs it before asking again. Show your own message (a dialog, for example) and let the user try again.

When the user refuses twice

After a second refusal Android stops showing the system dialog: asking again returns NOT_GRANTED at once. The only way to get the permission then is that the user enables it in the settings of the app, so offer a button that opens them.

docs.title: The manager
docs.text:
The screen creates the manager with rememberEmaPermissionManager(). In a @Preview it returns a manager that grants everything, so your previews don't open system dialogs.

val permissionManager = rememberEmaPermissionManager()

These are its functions. The ones that ask are suspend (they wait for the user), so call them from a coroutine:

Function What it does isPermissionGranted(permission) Is it granted right now? Returns a PermissionState. Doesn't ask anything. areAllPermissionsGranted(a, b) true if all of them are granted. Doesn't ask. shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(permission) true if Android recommends explaining before asking. Doesn't ask. requestPermission(permission) Asks for one permission and returns its PermissionState. requestMultiplePermission(a, b) Asks for several at once and returns a Map<String, PermissionState>. 
if (permissionManager.isPermissionGranted(Manifest.permission.CAMERA) == PermissionState.GRANTED) {
    openCamera()
}

One request at a time

Android cancels a request made while another one is on screen: it returns NOT_GRANTED (an empty map for several permissions) instead of waiting. Never launch two requests together.

docs.title: The quick way: ask from the screen
docs.text:
If the answer only matters to the screen, you can ask from a coroutine, with no ViewModel involved:

val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()

Button(onClick = {
    scope.launch {
        when (permissionManager.requestPermission(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)) {
            PermissionState.GRANTED -> openCamera()
            else -> showMessage("The camera is needed to take the photo")
        }
    }
}) { Text("Take photo") }

It works, but the decision (what happens when the user says no?) now lives in the screen, where it can't be tested without a device. When the answer changes what the screen shows or does, use the next section.

docs.title: The Emanate way: ask from the ViewModel
docs.text: We are going to build a screen that needs the location. The user presses Allow, Android asks, and the screen shows whether the permission was granted. If the user refuses once, we show an explanation.

docs.title: Step 1: the state and the actions
docs.text:
The state only says "a permission is being requested" and "the permission is granted". These are plain booleans: the ViewModel never touches Android.

data class LocationState(
    val requestingPermission: Boolean = false,   // true while the permission has to be requested
    val locationGranted: Boolean = false
) : EmaState

sealed interface LocationAction : EmaAction {
    data object AllowClicked : LocationAction                                           // the user pressed Allow
    data class PermissionAnswered(val permissionState: PermissionState) : LocationAction  // Android answered
}

sealed interface LocationEvent : EmaEvent {
    data object PermissionRationaleNeeded : LocationEvent
}

docs.title: Step 2: the ViewModel
docs.text:
class LocationViewModel : EmaViewModel<LocationState, LocationAction, LocationEvent>(LocationState()) {

    override fun setup() = source {
        reducers {
            add<LocationAction> { action ->
                when (action) {
                    is LocationAction.AllowClicked -> state.copy(requestingPermission = true)
                    is LocationAction.PermissionAnswered -> state.copy(
                        // The request is done, so it must not be executed again
                        requestingPermission = false,
                        locationGranted = action.permissionState == PermissionState.GRANTED
                    )
                }
            }
        }
        sideEffects {
            add<LocationAction.PermissionAnswered> { action ->
                if (action.permissionState == PermissionState.NOT_GRANTED_SHOULD_EXPLAIN) {
                    publish(LocationEvent.PermissionRationaleNeeded)
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

Read it as a conversation:

  • AllowClicked → "I need the permission": the reducer turns requestingPermission on.
  • PermissionAnswered → "here is the answer": the reducer turns requestingPermission off (very important, see the warning below) and stores whether it was granted.
  • If Android recommends an explanation, the side effect publishes an event so the screen can show it.

docs.title: Step 3: the screen executes the request
docs.text:
The screen watches requestingPermission. Each time it changes, a LaunchedEffect runs and asks Android:

@Composable
override fun onState(state: LocationState, actions: EmaActionDispatcher<LocationAction>) {
    val permissionManager = rememberEmaPermissionManager()
    val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()

    LaunchedEffect(state.requestingPermission) {
        val request = if (state.requestingPermission) {
            // When the user answers, the answer is dispatched as an action
            EmaPermissionRequest.createRequest { actions.dispatch(LocationAction.PermissionAnswered(it)) }
        } else {
            // "Nothing to do": the manager ignores it
            EmaPermissionRequest.cancelRequest()
        }
        permissionManager.handleRequest(request, scope, Manifest.permission.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION)
    }

    Column {
        Text(if (state.locationGranted) "Location allowed" else "Location not allowed")
        Button(onClick = { actions.dispatch(LocationAction.AllowClicked) }) { Text("Allow") }
    }
}

What each piece does:

Piece Its job LaunchedEffect(state.requestingPermission) Runs the block every time the flag changes: once when it turns true, and once when it turns false. EmaPermissionRequest.createRequest { ... } A request with a callback. The callback receives the PermissionState chosen by the user. EmaPermissionRequest.cancelRequest() The "nothing to do" request. handleRequest ignores it. It is what runs when the flag is false. permissionManager.handleRequest(request, scope, permission) If the request is real, it asks Android in scope and calls the callback with the answer.

Let's follow what happens when the user presses Allow:

# What happens Who 1 The user presses Allow. The screen sends AllowClicked. Screen 2 The reducer returns requestingPermission = true. ViewModel 3 The flag changed, so the LaunchedEffect runs and calls handleRequest. Android shows its dialog. Screen 4 The user chooses. The callback sends PermissionAnswered(GRANTED) (or another state). Screen 5 The reducer returns requestingPermission = false and locationGranted = true. The LaunchedEffect runs again, but now with cancelRequest(). ViewModel

Don't forget to turn the flag off

If PermissionAnswered leaves requestingPermission = true, the flag never changes again, the LaunchedEffect doesn't run, and the next press of Allow does nothing. The reducer of the answer always sets it back to false.

docs.title: Step 4: explain when Android recommends it
docs.text:
The side effect of Step 2 published PermissionRationaleNeeded. Handle it like any other event, for example opening a dialog that explains why the app needs the location, with a button that asks again:

sealed interface LocationDialog {
    data object WhyLocation : LocationDialog
}

// Reducer
is LocationAction.PermissionAnswered -> state.copy(
    requestingPermission = false,
    locationGranted = action.permissionState == PermissionState.GRANTED,
    dialog = if (action.permissionState == PermissionState.NOT_GRANTED_SHOULD_EXPLAIN) {
        LocationDialog.WhyLocation
    } else {
        null
    }
)

Here dialog is a new nullable field of LocationState, as explained in Dialogs. The "Try again" button of that dialog dispatches AllowClicked and the cycle starts again.

docs.title: Testing it without a device
docs.text:
The answer of the user is just an action, so a test can simulate every outcome without Android:

@Test
fun `a refused permission asks for an explanation`() = runTest {
    val viewModel = LocationViewModel()
    val recorder = viewModel.record()

    viewModel.dispatch(LocationAction.AllowClicked)
    recorder.assertState { it.requestingPermission }

    viewModel.dispatch(LocationAction.PermissionAnswered(PermissionState.NOT_GRANTED_SHOULD_EXPLAIN))
    advanceUntilIdle()

    recorder.assertState { !it.requestingPermission && !it.locationGranted }
    recorder.assertEvents(LocationEvent.PermissionRationaleNeeded)
}

See Testing for how to set up useTestConfiguration().

docs.title: Several permissions at once
docs.text:
To ask for more than one permission in a single system dialog, use the multiple versions. The callback receives a Map with the answer of each permission:

LaunchedEffect(state.requestingPermissions) {
    val request = if (state.requestingPermissions) {
        EmaMultiplePermissionRequest.createRequest { answers: Map<String, PermissionState> ->
            actions.dispatch(CaptureAction.PermissionsAnswered(answers))
        }
    } else {
        EmaMultiplePermissionRequest.cancelRequest()
    }
    permissionManager.handleRequestMultiple(
        request, scope,
        Manifest.permission.CAMERA, Manifest.permission.RECORD_AUDIO
    )
}

// In the reducer
val allGranted = action.answers.values.all { it == PermissionState.GRANTED }

docs.title: Location
docs.text:
Location has its own shortcuts, because it has some special rules:

Function Use requestCoarseLocationPermission() Approximate location. requestFineLocationPermission() Precise location. isLocationCoarseGranted(), isLocationFineGranted(), isLocationBackgroundGranted() Check without asking.
  • Ask for the precise location with requestFineLocationPermission(), not with requestPermission: depending on the Android version it must be requested together with the approximate one, and the function does it for you.
  • The background location (requestBackgroundLocationPermission(infoDialogType) of EmaAndroidPermissionManager) needs the precise one first. On recent Android versions the user grants it in the settings of the system, and infoDialogType decides the explanation shown before opening them: InfoDialogType.Default(title, message), or InfoDialogType.CustomDialog(alertDialog, onAcceptClickListener) to show your own dialog.

docs.title: Good practices
docs.text:
• Ask when it is needed, not at startup. Request the camera when the user taps Take photo, not when the app opens. People accept more when they understand why.
  • Always handle the refusal. The screen must still make sense without the permission.
  • Mind the system settings. If the user leaves the app to enable a permission there, Android may kill the process meanwhile. A backup keeps what they had typed.

docs.title: Compose screens
docs.text:
An Emanate screen splits the work between three pieces, so that each one has a single job:

Piece Job Example The ViewModel Holds the state and decides what happens when the user does something. It knows nothing about Compose. HomeViewModel The screen content (EmaScreenContent) Draws the state with Compose and reports what the user does. It keeps no data of its own. HomeScreenContent The registration (emaScreen) The glue. It creates the ViewModel, connects it to the content and to the lifecycle, puts the screen in your navigation graph and receives its events. The NavHost block

The information always travels the same way. In the home screen of the sample, the admin taps the button to create a user:

  1. The user taps Create, and the screen content sends the action CreateClicked.
  2. The ViewModel decides what that means. Whenever its state changes, the screen content draws it again.
  3. Here the answer is a one-off: the ViewModel publishes the event CreateClicked, and the onEvent of emaScreen opens the next screen.

The screen never changes the state itself: it only sends actions and draws whatever state the ViewModel gives it. Because of that, the same content can be shown in a preview, in a test or in a real app without changes.
