This page follows the life of a screen, from writing it to using it. You need the emanate-android and emanate-compose-android artifacts. To register the screens in a Navigation Compose graph, as in the examples, you also need emanate-compose-android-nav2: the other artifacts don't depend on any navigation library.

docs.title: Screen content
docs.text:
This is the part you will write most often: the Compose code of the screen. You create one class that implements EmaScreenContent and fill in onState, which receives the current state and draws it. When the user presses a button, you do not change anything: you send an action with actions.dispatch(...), and the ViewModel answers with a new state that makes onState run again.

class HomeScreenContent : EmaScreenContent<HomeState, HomeAction> {

    @Composable
    override fun onState(
        state: HomeState,
        actions: EmaActionDispatcher<HomeAction>
    ) {
        // Draw the state. Send user input with actions.dispatch(...)
    }
}

EmaScreenContent<S, A> takes the type of the state and the type of the actions, and has two members:

Member Purpose onState(state, actions) Required. Draws the state. It is a @Composable. onBack(state): A? The action to send when back is pressed, or null. See Back handling. Optional.

The screen content doesn't receive the events: they are handled where the screen is registered, as explained in Handling the events.

Keep the screen content free of state: it is a stateless description, created once per screen. Anything that must survive belongs in the state of the ViewModel.

docs.title: Registering the screen
docs.text:
A screen content on its own is just a description: nothing shows it yet. Registering it means adding it as a destination of your NavHost, as you would with Compose Navigation's composable(...), but with emaScreen, which also creates the ViewModel and wires everything together. This is also where you decide what happens when the ViewModel sends an event, such as navigating to another screen. emaScreen is in the emanate-compose-android-nav2 artifact. If you use another navigation, place the screen with EmaScreen, which is in emanate-compose-android.

NavHost(
    navController = navController,
    startDestination = HomeScreenContent::class.routeId
) {
    emaScreen(
        screenContent = HomeScreenContent(),
        viewModel = { get<HomeViewModel>() },
        onEvent = { navigator.handleHomeEvent(it) { /* show the message */ } }
    )
}
Parameter Purpose screenContent The screen content. viewModel A lambda that creates the ViewModel. It is called once, when the screen is opened, and receives the EmaStateStore of the screen for a backup. See Dependency injection. onEvent Receives every event of the screen. See Handling the events. routeId The route. By default ScreenContent::class.routeId, which is unique per class. initializerSupport How to read the initializer from the route. See Navigation. transitionAnimation EmaAnimTransition(enterTransition, exitTransition, popEnterTransition, popExitTransition). The pop transitions default to the enter and exit ones.

The parameters you will use most are the first three. The rest have a default value, so add them only when you need them. For example, a screen that enters sliding from the right:

emaScreen(
    screenContent = ProfileCreationScreenContent(),
    viewModel = { get<ProfileCreationViewModel>() },
    transitionAnimation = EmaAnimTransition(
        enterTransition = { slideInHorizontally { width -> width } },
        exitTransition = { slideOutHorizontally { width -> width } }
    ),
    onEvent = { navigator.handleProfileCreationEvent(it) }
)

docs.title: Showing a screen as a dialog
docs.text:
Some screens are shown over the previous one, in a dialog, instead of replacing it. Register them with emaDialog instead of emaScreen. Everything else is the same: the screen content, the ViewModel, the events and the initializer of the route. Only the transitions change, as a dialog has none, for dialogProperties, the DialogProperties of Compose:

emaDialog(
    screenContent = FilterScreenContent(),
    viewModel = { get<FilterViewModel>() },
    dialogProperties = DialogProperties(usePlatformDefaultWidth = false),
    onEvent = { navigator.handleFilterEvent(it) }
)

You open it like any other screen, with navController.navigate(FilterScreenContent::class.routeId).

This is a destination of the graph that looks like a dialog. For a small dialog inside a screen, like a confirmation, use the state instead: see Dialogs.

docs.title: Handling the events
docs.text:
An event is something that must happen once, like showing a toast or opening another screen, as opposed to the state, which is always there. Every event of the screen arrives at one place: the onEvent lambda of emaScreen. After it returns, the event is consumed and it will not arrive again.

onEvent is written in the graph, inside your activity or composable, so everything an event may need is at hand: the NavController or the navigator to navigate, and the Context to show a toast or open another app.

val context = LocalContext.current

NavHost(navController, startDestination = ProfileCreationScreenContent::class.routeId) {
    emaScreen(
        screenContent = ProfileCreationScreenContent(),
        viewModel = { get<ProfileCreationViewModel>() },
        onEvent = { event ->
            when (event) {
                ProfileCreationEvent.DialogConfirmationAccepted -> navController.navigateBack()
                is ProfileCreationEvent.ProfileSaved ->
                    Toast.makeText(context, "Profile saved", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
            }
        }
    )
}

As every event arrives at the same when, the compiler warns you when a new event is not handled. When the when grows, move it to a function of your navigator, as the sample does with navigator.handleHomeEvent(it).

onEvent must return quickly: the next events wait for it. Navigating or showing a toast is immediate. For something that takes time, like a snackbar, launch it in a coroutine scope of yours:

val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
val snackbarHostState = remember { SnackbarHostState() }

NavHost(navController, startDestination = ProfileCreationScreenContent::class.routeId) {
    emaScreen(
        screenContent = ProfileCreationScreenContent(),
        viewModel = { get<ProfileCreationViewModel>() },
        onEvent = { event ->
            when (event) {
                is ProfileCreationEvent.ProfileSaved -> scope.launch { snackbarHostState.showSnackbar("Saved") }
                ProfileCreationEvent.DialogConfirmationAccepted -> navController.navigateBack()
            }
        }
    )
}

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
A screen goes through moments: it is created, it appears, the user leaves to another app, it comes back, it is destroyed. The ViewModel often needs to know, for example to load data when the screen appears or to stop listening to something when it is paused. You do not have to observe the lifecycle yourself: the screen does it and passes each moment on to the ViewModel.

The screen connects the ViewModel to the lifecycle of its destination:

Lifecycle event The ViewModel receives ON_CREATE, the first time The EmaInitializer of the screen ON_START EmaLifecycle.Started ON_RESUME EmaLifecycle.Resumed ON_PAUSE EmaLifecycle.Paused ON_STOP EmaLifecycle.Stopped The screen leaves the composition EmaLifecycle.Paused and EmaLifecycle.Stopped The destination is removed EmaLifecycle.Destroyed, and it is closed

The state is collected with collectAsStateWithLifecycle and the events while the lifecycle is STARTED.

docs.title: Previews
docs.text:
The @Preview of Android Studio draws a composable without running the app, which makes designing the UI much faster. But a preview cannot create a real ViewModel, so you give it a state by hand and see how the screen looks with it. Writing one preview per interesting state (empty, loading, error...) is a cheap way to check them all.

Inside the IDE preview there is no ViewModel, so call onState directly with a state and an empty dispatcher:

@Preview
@Composable
private fun PreviewNormal() {
    EmaSampleTheme {
        ProfileCreationScreenContent().onState(
            state = ProfileCreationState("Carlos", "Mateo"),
            actions = EmaActionDispatcher.EMPTY
        )
    }
}

docs.title: Using a screen without a navigation graph
docs.text:
emaScreen needs a NavHost. But not every app uses Navigation Compose: an activity may show a single screen, or you may want an Emanate screen as just a part of a bigger layout, like a counter inside a page. For those cases there is EmaScreen, a composable that you place wherever you want, like a Text or a Column.

EmaScreen is in fact what emaScreen draws inside each destination, so it does the same work: it creates the ViewModel, connects it to the lifecycle, draws the state with the screen content, sends the back button actions and passes every event to onEvent. The only thing missing is the graph.

docs.title: A screen in an activity
docs.text:
The most common case: an activity that shows one Emanate screen and nothing else. Imagine a counter with a + button that warns the user when it reaches 10.

class CounterActivity : ComponentActivity() {

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContent {
            EmaSampleTheme {
                EmaScreen(
                    vm = { CounterViewModel() },
                    screenContent = CounterScreenContent(),
                    onEvent = { event ->
                        when (event) {
                            CounterEvent.LimitReached ->
                                Toast.makeText(this, "You reached 10", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
                        }
                    }
                )
            }
        }
    }
}

The parameters are the ones of emaScreen, with shorter names:

Parameter Purpose vm A lambda that creates the ViewModel. It is called only the first time, as in emaScreen. screenContent The screen content. onEvent Receives every event of the screen, as in Handling the events. initializer The initializer of the screen. Here there is no route to read it from, so you pass it directly. Optional. previewRenderState The state to draw in a preview. See Previews of a bigger layout. Optional.

For example, to open the counter starting at 5, pass the initializer yourself:

EmaScreen(
    initializer = CounterInitializer(start = 5),
    vm = { CounterViewModel() },
    screenContent = CounterScreenContent(),
    onEvent = { /* ... */ }
)

docs.title: A screen inside a bigger layout
docs.text:
As EmaScreen is a composable, it can be one piece of a page. Here the counter sits under a title and over a button that is not part of it:

@Composable
fun DashboardPage(onSettingsClicked: () -> Unit) {
    Column {
        Text("Dashboard", style = MaterialTheme.typography.headlineMedium)

        EmaScreen(
            vm = { CounterViewModel() },
            screenContent = CounterScreenContent(),
            onEvent = { /* ... */ }
        )

        Button(onClick = onSettingsClicked) { Text("Settings") }
    }
}

The ViewModel lives as long as the activity (or the destination of the graph) that contains the page, not as long as the composable. If the counter is inside an if and disappears, its ViewModel receives Paused and Stopped, and keeps its state: when the counter appears again, it shows the same number.

docs.title: Previews of a bigger layout
docs.text:
previewRenderState is the state that the screen shows instead of the real one when it is drawn in the preview of Android Studio:

Where the screen is drawn What it shows In the app, on a device The real state, the one of the ViewModel. previewRenderState is ignored. In the preview of Android Studio previewRenderState. The ViewModel is not even created.

You need it because a preview cannot create the ViewModel, so without previewRenderState the screen has no state to draw and its space stays empty. With it, you see the whole page as it will look:

@Composable
fun DashboardPage() {
    Column {
        Text("Dashboard")
        EmaScreen(
            vm = { CounterViewModel() },
            screenContent = CounterScreenContent(),
            onEvent = { /* ... */ },
            // Only for the preview: the app shows the real count of the ViewModel
            previewRenderState = CounterState(count = 3)
        )
    }
}

@Preview
@Composable
private fun PreviewDashboard() {
    // The title and a counter with the number 3
    DashboardPage()
}

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
An action is something the user did: "pulled to refresh", "wrote a query", "confirmed the dialog". Actions go from the view to the ViewModel.

sealed interface HomeAction : EmaAction {

    data object RefreshRequested : HomeAction
    data class QueryWritten(val query: String) : HomeAction
    data class FriendClicked(val friend: User) : HomeAction
    data object ErrorAccepted : HomeAction
}

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
Name actions after what the user did, in the past tense, not after what the ViewModel should do. QueryWritten is better than UpdateQuery: the view reports the fact and the ViewModel decides what to do with it.

Use a sealed interface so that when is exhaustive. When you add an action the compiler tells you everywhere you must handle it.

docs.title: Handling actions
docs.text:
Declare in the setup of the ViewModel the middlewares, reducers and side effects of each type of action. With the sealed type, a reducer handles every action of the screen in an exhaustive when, and a side effect can handle a single action:

override fun setup() = source {
    reducers {
        add<HomeAction> { action ->
            when (action) {
                is HomeAction.QueryWritten -> state.copy(query = action.query)
                is HomeAction.ErrorAccepted -> state.copy(dialog = null)
                // ...
            }
        }
    }
    sideEffects {
        add<HomeAction.RefreshRequested> { /* ... */ }
    }
}

See The setup. The public entry point of the ViewModel is dispatch(action), so a view can only communicate through actions and cannot call arbitrary functions of the ViewModel.

docs.title: Actions are also results
docs.text:
The side effects report what happened with actions too, so the reducers can apply it. Group them in a sealed type inside the actions of the screen, called SideEffects, so it is clear that only the ViewModel sends them. Name each action after what happened (QueryLoaded):

sealed interface HomeAction : EmaAction {
    // ...

    // The results of the search, dispatched by its side effect
    sealed interface SideEffects : HomeAction {
        data object QueryStarted : SideEffects
        data class QueryLoaded(val friends: List<User>) : SideEffects
        data object QueryFailed : SideEffects
    }
}

As every change of the state comes from an action, the log of the actions tells the whole story of the screen, and a test can check it step by step.

docs.title: Dispatching from the view
docs.text:
A Compose screen content receives the state and an EmaActionDispatcher, the same one for the whole life of the screen, so it doesn't cause unnecessary recompositions. Every callback of the UI only reports what the user did with actions.dispatch:

class HomeScreenContent : EmaScreenContent<HomeState, HomeAction> {

    @Composable
    override fun onState(state: HomeState, actions: EmaActionDispatcher<HomeAction>) {
        Column {
            // The user writes a query
            OutlinedTextField(
                value = state.query,
                onValueChange = { query -> actions.dispatch(HomeAction.QueryWritten(query)) }
            )
            // The user asks for a refresh
            Button(onClick = { actions.dispatch(HomeAction.RefreshRequested) }) {
                Text(text = "Refresh")
            }
            // The user clicks a friend
            FriendList(
                friends = state.friends,
                onFriendClick = { friend -> actions.dispatch(HomeAction.FriendClicked(friend)) }
            )
        }
        // The user accepts the error dialog
        if (state.dialog == HomeDialog.LoadError) {
            AlertDialog(
                onDismissRequest = { actions.dispatch(HomeAction.ErrorAccepted) },
                confirmButton = {
                    TextButton(onClick = { actions.dispatch(HomeAction.ErrorAccepted) }) { Text(text = "OK") }
                },
                text = { Text(text = "The friends couldn't be loaded") }
            )
        }
    }
}

The callbacks never change the state nor decide what happens next: the ViewModel does, in its reducers and side effects. Child composables like FriendList receive plain callbacks, so they don't depend on Emanate and can be reused or previewed on their own.

For previews use EmaActionDispatcher.EMPTY, which ignores every action.

docs.title: Special action types
docs.text:
Type Use EmaAction The actions of a screen. Your actions extend this. EmaInitializer The data a screen starts with. See Initializers. EmaLifecycle The lifecycle of the view: Started, Resumed, Paused, Stopped and Destroyed. See ViewModel. EmaRestoreState The values restored by a backup after the death of the process. EmaAction.EMPTY The action type of a screen without actions.

Any of them can be handled by the middlewares, reducers and side effects, like the actions of the screen.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Every Emanate screen is made of the same pieces, and every action follows the same path through them.

  1. The view sends an action with dispatch.
  2. The middlewares of its type decide its path: let it continue, change it, delay it or stop it.
  3. The reducers of its type return the next state, which the view renders.
  4. The side effects of its type run the business logic asynchronously. They report the result by dispatching new actions, which go through the same path, or by publishing events.
  5. The view handles each event once, for example to navigate or show a message.
Piece Responsibility Depends on the platform? EmaState What the screen looks like right now. No EmaAction What the user did, or the result of some work. No EmaEvent What happened and must be handled once. No EmaViewModel Handles each action with its middlewares, reducers and side effects. No View Renders the state, handles events and sends actions. Yes

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
1. The view only renders and reports. It renders the state and sends actions. It never changes the state or holds business logic.
  2. The state only changes in the reducers. They are pure functions: the state is replaced, never mutated.
  3. The business logic lives in the side effects. They call use cases and report back with actions, so every change of the state is visible as an action.
  4. Anything that lasts belongs in the state; anything that happens once belongs in an event. A loading spinner or a validation error is state. A snackbar or a navigation is an event.
  5. Events describe what happened, not what to do. Name them FriendSelected, not OpenProfile. The receiver decides the reaction: the same event could open a screen on a phone and update a pane on a tablet.
  6. Repositories are only accessed through use cases (a recommendation, see Recommendations).

docs.title: State or event?
docs.text:
This is the question you will ask most often when building a feature.

Question If yes → Should it still be there after the screen is recreated? State Should it show again if the user comes back to the screen? State Is it a fact about something that just happened? Event Would showing it twice be a bug (toast, navigation)? Event

Examples from a home screen:

What Where The query typed in the search field State (HomeState.query) The loading indicator of the list State (HomeState.isLoading) "The friends couldn't be loaded" dialog State (HomeState.dialog) "12 friends" message Event (HomeEvent.FriendsUpdated) Opening the profile of a friend Event (HomeEvent.FriendSelected)

docs.title: Broadcasts
docs.text:
A broadcast sends an action from one screen to other screens. The typical case is a result.

Imagine an app with a Home screen that shows a list of friends, and a button that opens a Profile screen, with a form to create a new friend. When the user saves the form, the Profile screen closes and the list of the Home screen, which was waiting behind it, must show the new friend.

The Profile screen doesn't know the Home screen, and it shouldn't. It only announces what happened ("a friend was created") and any screen that is interested reacts to it. That announcement is a broadcast.

Any ViewModel that listens to the type of the action receives it as one more action of its own, so it handles it with its usual middlewares, reducers and side effects. There are no shared ViewModels, no result APIs of the platform and no casts: the result is a typed data class.

docs.title: When to use a broadcast
docs.text:
A ViewModel never holds a reference to another one, so a broadcast is the way to communicate ViewModels that are not directly linked: the one that sends doesn't know who receives, and the one that receives doesn't know who sent.

You want to... Use Send a result or a notification to other screens A broadcast Tell the view of the same screen to do something once An event

docs.title: In four steps
docs.text:
1. Declare the action, next to the actions of the screen that sends it:

sealed interface ProfileBroadcast : EmaAction {
    data class FriendCreated(val friend: User) : ProfileBroadcast
}

2. Send it from a side effect of the sender, with broadcast:

// ProfileViewModel
sideEffects {
    add<ProfileAction.SaveClicked> {
        broadcast(ProfileBroadcast.FriendCreated(state.friend))
        publish(ProfileEvent.Saved)  // The navigator closes the screen
    }
}

3. Listen to its type in the broadcasts block of the receiver:

// HomeViewModel
override fun setup() = source {
    broadcasts {
        listen<ProfileBroadcast.FriendCreated>()
    }
    // ...
}

4. Handle it like any other action:

// HomeViewModel
reducers {
    add<ProfileBroadcast.FriendCreated> { action -> state.copy(friends = state.friends + action.friend) }
}
sideEffects {
    add<ProfileBroadcast.FriendCreated> { action -> publish(HomeEvent.FriendAdded(action.friend)) }
}

Don't forget to listen to the broadcast

Without listen<Type>(), the receiver never gets the action, and nothing fails: no error, no log. The screen just doesn't update.

docs.title: How it is delivered
docs.text:
• At once, to every ViewModel that listens to the type at that moment. The ViewModels of the previous screens are alive in the back stack, so they receive it.
  • To any number of receivers. Every ViewModel that listens to the type receives the action.
  • Only while the receiver exists. Its listener is removed when it is closed, with the rest of its work.
  • In memory. It is not saved if the process is killed.
  • Lost if nobody listens, unless it is kept. See below.

docs.title: Keeping it until it is received
docs.text:
With keepUntilReceived = true, an action that nobody is listening to is kept and delivered to the first ViewModel that listens to its type. Only the last one of each class is kept. If someone is listening, it is delivered at once, as usual.

broadcast(ProfileBroadcast.FriendCreated(state.friend), keepUntilReceived = true)

It covers a screen that doesn't exist yet. For example, when the system kills the app in the background, it restores only the current screen: the ViewModel of the previous one is created when the user goes back to it. Without keeping the result, it would be lost.

docs.title: Who can receive it
docs.text: The actions go through the broadcaster of the configuration. By default every ViewModel of the app shares the same one. A library built with Emanate can give its ViewModels their own broadcaster, so they only talk to each other. See Libraries and SDKs.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
An event is something that happened in the feature and that the view must handle once: show a message, open another screen, close the screen.

sealed interface HomeEvent : EmaEvent {
    data class FriendsUpdated(val count: Int) : HomeEvent
    data class FriendAdded(val friend: User) : HomeEvent
    data class FriendSelected(val friend: User) : HomeEvent
}

docs.title: Publishing events
docs.text:
Events are published from the side effects of the ViewModel, with publish:

sideEffects {
    add<HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded> { action -> publish(HomeEvent.FriendsUpdated(action.friends.size)) }
    add<HomeAction.FriendClicked> { action -> publish(HomeEvent.FriendSelected(action.friend)) }
}

An event arrives after the actions dispatched before it, so the view sees the state they produced.

docs.title: Handling events
docs.text:
The view handles each event once, in the order they were published. A Compose screen handles all of them in one place: the onEvent lambda of emaScreen, in the navigation graph. There the NavController, the navigator and the Context are at hand, so it can navigate, show a message or do anything else:

class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContent {
            val navController = rememberNavController()
            val navigator = remember { HomeNavigator(navController) }
            NavHost(navController, startDestination = HomeScreenContent::class.routeId) {
                emaScreen(
                    screenContent = HomeScreenContent(),
                    viewModel = { get<HomeViewModel>() },
                    onEvent = { event ->
                        when (event) {
                            is HomeEvent.FriendSelected -> navigator.goToProfile(event.friend)
                            is HomeEvent.FriendsUpdated -> toast("${event.count} friends")
                            is HomeEvent.FriendAdded -> toast("${event.friend.name} is now your friend")
                        }
                    }
                )
            }
        }
    }

    private fun toast(message: String) = Toast.makeText(this, message, Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
}

As every event arrives at the same when, the compiler warns you when a new event is not handled. If the when grows, move it to a function of the navigator. See Compose screens.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
Events say what happened, never what to do. The receiver decides the reaction.

Prefer Avoid Why FriendSelected(user) OpenProfile(user) The ViewModel does not know that selecting means navigating. LoginSuccess(user) GoToHome Which screen follows is the navigator's decision. CloseClicked CloseScreen The view could also just hide a pane. FriendAdded(user) ShowToast(user) It could be a toast, a snackbar or nothing at all.

A good test: the name still makes sense if you replace the screen's UI completely.

docs.title: Delivery rules
docs.text:
• Once. After onEvent returns, the event is consumed. It is not replayed when the view is recreated.
  • Not lost. Events are queued in the ViewModel until a view is able to receive them. If you publish an event while the screen is in the background, or while it is being recreated, it is delivered afterwards.
  • In order. Several pending events are delivered as a batch, in the order they were published.
  • Equal events. While an event is waiting to be delivered, publishing an equal one does nothing, so a double tap does not show the same message twice. Once the view has handled it, an equal event is a new one and is delivered again. To queue an equal event while the first one is still waiting, pass allowDuplicated = true:
publish(HomeEvent.FriendAdded(ana), allowDuplicated = true)
  • Only while the screen is visible. Compose screens receive events while the lifecycle is STARTED.
  • Not persisted. Events live in the ViewModel, so they survive configuration changes but not process death.

Keep onEvent short. The events are delivered one after another, and an event is consumed when its onEvent returns. Navigating or showing a toast is immediate. For something that takes time, like a snackbar that waits for the user, launch it in a coroutine scope of yours, such as the one of rememberCoroutineScope(), so the next events do not wait for it. Send long-running work back to the ViewModel as an action.

docs.title: Events or state
docs.text: If it must be there when the user comes back, it is state, not an event. See the table in Architecture.

docs.title: Screens with no events
docs.text:
A screen that never publishes events uses EmaEvent.EMPTY as its event type, and its onEvent does nothing:

class SettingsViewModel : EmaViewModel<SettingsState, SettingsAction, EmaEvent.EMPTY>(SettingsState()) {
    // ...
}

emaScreen(
    screenContent = SettingsScreenContent(),
    viewModel = { SettingsViewModel() },
    onEvent = {}
)

In the same way, EmaState.EMPTY is the state of a screen with no state, and EmaAction.EMPTY the actions of a screen the user can't interact with. A screen with no state, actions nor events has no logic: draw it with a plain composable, without Emanate.

docs.title: Middlewares
docs.text:
A middleware is a checkpoint: it sees an action before the reducers and the side effects, and decides what happens to it.

In the middleware Effect next() Continues as it is, to the next middleware and then to the reducers. next(other) Is replaced: other continues instead. nextAfter { } Continues later, when the block finishes. The screen keeps working meanwhile. Doesn't call next Stops here. The reducers and the side effects never see it. state The current state of the screen, readable before and after next(). dispatch(action) Dispatches a new action.

Most screens don't need middlewares. They shine for things that apply to many actions and that the business logic shouldn't know: analytics, logs, debounce, feature flags, simulated latency in a test build...

docs.title: Your first middleware
docs.text:
Middlewares are declared in the middlewares block of the setup, for a type of action. This one logs every action of the screen and lets it continue:

middlewares {
    add<HomeAction> { action ->
        println("The user did $action")
        next()
    }
}

Remember call next, only once

If you forget it, the action stops there and the screen seems to ignore it. If you call it twice, the app fails with an error, because an action can only continue once.

docs.title: Stopping an action
docs.text:
Not calling next stops the action. For example, to ignore taps on a feature that is disabled:

middlewares {
    add<HomeAction.FriendClicked> {
        if (featureFlags.profilesEnabled) next()
    }
}

docs.title: Replacing an action
docs.text:
next(other) lets another action continue instead of the received one:

middlewares {
    // A blank query is the same as clearing the search
    add<HomeAction.QueryWritten> { action ->
        if (action.query.isBlank()) next(HomeAction.SearchCleared) else next()
    }
}

docs.title: Waiting: delays and debounce
docs.text:
nextAfter lets the action continue when its block finishes, without blocking the screen. Inside the block, stop() discards the action.

With an id, a new nextAfter with the same id cancels the one that is still waiting. That is a debounce: while the user keeps typing, only the last query continues.

middlewares {
    add<HomeAction.QueryWritten> { action ->
        nextAfter(id = "search") {
            delay(300)
            if (action.query.length < 2) stop()
        }
    }
}

For a fixed delay, middlewareDelayOf creates the middleware for you:

middlewares {
    // Every refresh waits two seconds.
    // This can be useful, for example, to see the loading state in a test build
    add(middlewareDelayOf(HomeAction.RefreshRequested::class, 2.seconds))
}

nextAfter also accepts a timeout: if the block doesn't finish in time, the block is cancelled, the action doesn't continue, and onTimeout runs instead. In this example, a refresh that takes more than one second is reported as a failure:

middlewares {
    add<HomeAction.RefreshRequested> {
        nextAfter(
            timeout = 1.seconds,
            onTimeout = { dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed) }
        ) {
            // A task that takes more than 1 second
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Reading the state
docs.text:
A middleware can read the state of the screen with state, before and after calling next(). It can't change it: the state only changes in the reducers. To change it, the middleware dispatches an action.

Before next(), state is the state the action finds, before the reducers apply it. Use it to decide the path of the action. For example, ignore the taps on a friend while a dialog is open:

middlewares {
    add<HomeAction.FriendClicked> {
        if (state.dialog == null) next()
    }
}

After next(), state is the new state: when next() returns, the rest of the middlewares and the reducers have run. Use it to see what the action changed. This middleware logs only the actions that changed the state:

middlewares(MiddlewarePosition.Last) {
    add<HomeAction> { action ->
        val before = state
        next()
        if (state != before) println("$action changed the state to $state")
    }
}

Note

After next(), the state is the new one only if no middleware after this one delays the action with nextAfter or stops it. With MiddlewarePosition.Last nothing can be in between, so it is always the new state.

While waiting, the block of nextAfter can also read state: it is the state at the moment it is read, after the wait, which can be different from the one the action found. This example waits a moment and only continues if no dialog has been opened meanwhile:

middlewares {
    add<HomeAction.QueryWritten> { action ->
        nextAfter(id = "search") {
            delay(300)
            if (state.dialog != null) stop()
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Where a middleware runs
docs.text:
By default the middlewares run in the order they are written. A block can place its middlewares before or after the rest, wherever it is written:

MiddlewarePosition Runs Use it for First Before the rest Deciding the path of every action first: a session check, a feature flag. InPlace (default) Where the block is written The middlewares of the screen. Last After the rest, right before the reducers Observing the new state: when next() returns, the reducers have run.

For example, this middleware runs before all the others and checks the session of the user. If the session is active, the action continues as usual; otherwise next() is not called, so the action stops and none of the pieces of the screen see it:

middlewares(MiddlewarePosition.First) {
    add<HomeAction> { if (session.isActive) next() }
}

The position is especially useful when you write plugins. A plugin is installed in many screens, so it can't depend on where it is written: with First it sees every action before the pieces of the screen, like the session check above, and with Last it sees the new state after the reducers, like the backup of the state.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
• Call next once, now or later with nextAfter.
  • Don't publish events. To tell the view something, dispatch an action with dispatch(action) and let a side effect publish the event.
  • Keep the business logic in the side effects. A middleware decides the path of the action; the work it starts belongs to a side effect.

docs.title: Middlewares as values
docs.text:
A middleware can also be created with middlewareOf or middlewareDelayOf, instead of being written inline. This would be how a middleware is implemented as value:

class HomeViewModel : EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(HomeState()) {

    private val blankQueryAsClear = middlewareOf(HomeAction.QueryWritten::class) { action ->
        if (action.query.isBlank()) next(HomeAction.SearchCleared) else next()
    }

    override fun setup() = source {
        middlewares { add(blankQueryAsClear) }
        // ...
    }
}

It could also be received in the constructor, so a QA build could add latency to the screen without touching it:

class HomeViewModel(
    private val tuning: List<EmaMiddleware<HomeState, HomeAction, *>> = emptyList()
) : EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(HomeState()) {

    override fun setup() = source {
        middlewares(MiddlewarePosition.First) { tuning.forEach { add(it) } }
        // ...
    }
}

See Dependency injection and environments.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
A plugin is a reusable setup: it groups a set of middlewares, reducers, side effects and broadcast listeners that work together, and any screen installs all of them in one line.

Use a plugin for a feature that many screens need, but that has nothing to do with what each screen does: analytics, a session check, a feature flag, the backup of the state... Without plugins, that code is copied in every ViewModel, or hidden in a base class that every screen must extend.

docs.title: Installing a plugin
docs.text:
Plugins are installed in the plugins block of the setup, with add:

override fun setup() = source {
    plugins {
        add(ScreenAnalytics<HomeState>(tracker, screen = "Home"))
    }
    reducers { /* ... */ }
}

Its pieces are added to the setup of the screen, where the plugins block is written, and work together with the pieces of the screen.

docs.title: Writing a plugin
docs.text:
A plugin implements EmaSourcePlugin and adds its pieces in install, with the same blocks as setup. This one tracks every action of the screen and when the screen is shown:

class ScreenAnalytics<S : EmaState>(private val tracker: Tracker, private val screen: String) :
    EmaSourcePlugin<S, Nothing> {

    override fun install(setup: SourceSetupScope<S, Nothing, Nothing>) {
        // A middleware sees every action of the screen before the reducers
        setup.middlewares {
            add<EmaAction> { action ->
                tracker.track(screen, action::class.simpleName.orEmpty())
                next()
            }
        }
        // A side effect reacts to the lifecycle of the screen
        setup.sideEffects {
            add<EmaLifecycle.Resumed> { tracker.screenShown(screen) }
        }
    }
}
  • What it needs, it receives in the constructor, like the tracker. It can't be installed without it.
  • S is the state of the screens where it can be installed. A generic S, as here, works in any screen; write it when installing it: ScreenAnalytics<HomeState>(...).
  • The second type is the type of the actions the plugin dispatches. Nothing means it dispatches none.

docs.title: A plugin with its own actions
docs.text:
A plugin can't publish events, because the events belong to each screen. To tell the screen something, it dispatches actions, and the screen decides what to do with them. Which actions it can dispatch is the second type of the plugin. Usually they are actions that the plugin defines, like the one below, so it works in any screen. A plugin written for one specific screen could also use the actions of that screen as its second type, but then it only works there.

This plugin stops the actions of the user when the session has expired, and tells the screen with SessionAction.Expired:

sealed interface SessionAction : EmaAction {
    data object Expired : SessionAction
}

class SessionGuard<S : EmaState>(private val session: Session) : EmaSourcePlugin<S, SessionAction> {

    override fun install(setup: SourceSetupScope<S, SessionAction, Nothing>) {
        setup.middlewares(MiddlewarePosition.First) {
            add<EmaAction> { action ->
                // The lifecycle and the actions of the plugin always continue
                if (action is EmaLifecycle || action is SessionAction || session.isActive) {
                    next()
                } else {
                    dispatch(SessionAction.Expired)
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

The screen installs it and reacts to its action like to any other:

override fun setup() = source {
    plugins {
        add(SessionGuard<HomeState>(session))
    }
    sideEffects {
        add<SessionAction.Expired> { publish(HomeEvent.SessionExpired) }
    }
}

docs.title: Where its pieces go
docs.text:
The pieces of a plugin run in an order that depends on their kind.

Reducers, side effects and broadcast listeners stay where the plugins block is written, in order with the pieces of the screen. Here, the plugin has a reducer and a side effect:

override fun setup() = source {
    reducers {
        add<HomeAction> { /* reducer 1 */ }
    }
    plugins {
        add(MyPlugin())  // Its reducer and its side effect go here
    }
    reducers {
        add<HomeAction> { /* reducer 3 */ }
    }
}

When an action arrives, the reducers run in this order: reducer 1, the one of the plugin and reducer 3. Each one receives the state returned by the previous one. The side effects are launched in the same order.

Middlewares can choose a position, wherever the plugin is installed: MiddlewarePosition.First to see every action before anything else, like the SessionGuard, or Last to see the new state of every action, like the backup. See Where a middleware runs. Here, the plugins are written after the middleware of the screen:

override fun setup() = source {
    middlewares {
        add<HomeAction> { /* middleware of the screen */ }
    }
    plugins {
        add(SessionGuard<HomeState>(session))  // Its middleware is First
        add(backup)                            // Its middleware is Last
    }
}

When an action arrives, the middlewares run in this order: the one of SessionGuard (First), the one of the screen and the one of the backup (Last). Then come the reducers. The position wins over the place where the plugin is written.

docs.title: An alternative: extension functions
docs.text:
A plugin can't publish events, because it doesn't know the events of the screen. For that, write an extension function of the setup and call it inside source { }: it has the state, the actions and the events of the screen.

They are also useful when a ViewModel gets big. Each function groups a subfeature of the screen, and the ViewModel only calls them. This one counts the loads that fail in a row, and after three of them the view suggests checking the connection:

fun SourceSetupScope<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>.suggestCheckingConnection() {
    reducers {
        // Counts the failures in a row, and starts again when a load works
        add<HomeAction.SideEffects> { action ->
            when (action) {
                is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed -> state.copy(failures = state.failures + 1)
                is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded -> state.copy(failures = 0)
                is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted -> state
            }
        }
    }
    sideEffects {
        // The reducer has already counted this failure
        add<HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed> {
            if (state.failures == 3) publish(HomeEvent.CheckConnection)
        }
    }
}

class HomeViewModel : EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(HomeState()) {

    override fun setup() = source {
        suggestCheckingConnection()
        reducers { /* ... */ }
        sideEffects { /* ... */ }
    }
}

docs.title: The plugins of Emanate
docs.text: • The backup of the state, created with backupOf, saves parts of the state and restores them after the system kills the app. See Surviving process death.

docs.title: Reducers
docs.text:
A reducer answers one question: given the current state and an action, what is the next state?

It is the only place where the state of a screen changes. Everything the user sees on the screen is the result of a reducer.

docs.title: Your first reducer
docs.text:
Reducers are declared in the reducers block of the setup of the ViewModel. add<Type> adds a reducer for the actions of that type, and its lambda returns the new state:

override fun setup() = source {
    reducers {
        add<HomeAction.QueryWritten> { action ->
            state.copy(query = action.query)
        }
    }
}

Inside the lambda you have:

Name What it is state The current state of the screen. action The action that arrived, already of its type.

The value the lambda returns becomes the new state, and the view draws it straight away.

docs.title: One reducer for the whole screen
docs.text:
With a sealed type of actions, a single reducer can handle every action of the screen with a when. The compiler checks that no action is forgotten: add a new action and it tells you where to handle it.

reducers {
    add<HomeAction> { action ->
        when (action) {
            is HomeAction.QueryWritten -> state.copy(query = action.query, errorQueryTooShort = false)
            is HomeAction.ErrorAccepted -> state.copy(dialog = null)
            is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted -> state.copy(isLoading = true)
            is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded -> state.copy(isLoading = false, friends = action.friends)
            is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed -> state.copy(isLoading = false, dialog = HomeDialog.LoadError)
            is HomeAction.RefreshRequested,
            is HomeAction.FriendClicked -> state
        }
    }
}

An action that doesn't change the state, like FriendClicked, returns state as it is. Something else will react to it: a side effect.

Both styles can be mixed: a big when for the screen, and small reducers for other types, like the initializer or a broadcast.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
A reducer is a pure function: with the same state and the same action, it always returns the same new state, and it does nothing else. That is what makes it easy to read and to test.

A reducer can A reducer can't Read state and the action Call use cases, repositories or the network Return a new state with copy Dispatch actions or publish events: dispatch doesn't even compile here Compute values from them Read the clock, random numbers or anything that changes on its own

Work like loading data or saving something goes in a side effect, which runs after the reducers and reports its result with a new action, that a reducer applies.

docs.title: Several reducers for the same action
docs.text:
When more than one reducer handles an action, they run in the order they were added, and each one receives the state returned by the previous one:

reducers {
    add<HomeAction.QueryWritten> { action -> state.copy(query = action.query) }
    // Receives the state with the new query
    add<HomeAction.QueryWritten> { state.copy(errorQueryTooShort = state.query.length == 1) }
}

docs.title: Reducers as values
docs.text:
A reducer can also be created with reducerOf, to declare it as a property, share it or receive it in the constructor, and added with add:

class HomeViewModel : EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(HomeState()) {

    private val queryReducer = reducerOf(HomeAction.QueryWritten::class) { action ->
        state.copy(query = action.query)
    }

    override fun setup() = source {
        reducers { add(queryReducer) }
    }
}

See Pieces are values.

docs.title: Testing a reducer
docs.text:
Dispatch the action and check the state:

viewModel.dispatch(HomeAction.QueryWritten("Ana"))

assertEquals("Ana", viewModel.stateFlow.value.query)

With emanate-test, record() keeps every state the reducers return, in order.

docs.title: Side effects
docs.text:
A side effect is the work that an action starts: loading data, saving something, calling a use case, waiting for a timer. It runs after the reducers of the action, so it already sees the new state, and it reports what happened in three ways:

When its work finishes, a side effect can't change the state nor the UI directly. It reports the result with one of these three functions, depending on what has to happen with it:

Use it to Call Example Result Save the result in the state dispatch(action) The friends were loaded: dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded(friends)) A reducer puts them in the state and the list shows them. Trigger a one-time UI action, like navigating or showing a message publish(event) The user clicked a friend: publish(HomeEvent.FriendSelected(friend)) The profile of the friend is opened. Notify other ViewModels broadcast(action) A friend was created: broadcast(ProfileBroadcast.FriendCreated(friend)) The ViewModels that listen to it receive it. See Broadcasts.

A side effect never changes the state by itself: it dispatches an action and a reducer applies it. That keeps every change of the state in one place, and visible as an action.

docs.title: Your first side effect
docs.text:
Side effects are declared in the sideEffects block of the setup, for a type of action. They are suspend, so they can call use cases directly:

sideEffects {
    add<HomeAction.RefreshRequested> {
        dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted)
        getFriendsUseCase(GetFriendsUseCase.Input(state.query))
            .onSuccess { friends -> dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded(friends)) }
            .onFailure { dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed) }
    }
}

Step by step:

  1. The user pulls to refresh, and the view dispatches RefreshRequested.
  2. The reducers of RefreshRequested run. Then this side effect starts.
  3. It dispatches Started: a reducer shows the loading indicator.
  4. It waits for the use case. The screen keeps working meanwhile.
  5. It dispatches Loaded or Failed: a reducer shows the list or the error dialog.

Inside the lambda you have state (always the latest one), the action that launched it, and dispatch, publish and broadcast.

docs.title: Publishing an event
docs.text:
When the view must do something once, like navigating or showing a message, publish an event:

sideEffects {
    add<HomeAction.FriendClicked> { action ->
        publish(HomeEvent.FriendSelected(action.friend))
    }
}

docs.title: When the same action arrives twice
docs.text:
What if the user taps "refresh" again while the first refresh is still running? You choose with concurrency:

concurrency What happens Use it for Every (default) Both run, at the same time. Independent work, like sending messages. Latest The running one is cancelled and the new one starts. A search: only the last query matters. Leading The new one is ignored while one is running. A button tapped twice: don't send it twice. 
sideEffects {
    add<HomeAction.RefreshRequested>(concurrency = SideEffectConcurrency.Leading) { /* ... */ }
    add<HomeAction.QueryWritten>(concurrency = SideEffectConcurrency.Latest) { /* ... */ }
}

docs.title: Giving up after some time
docs.text:
With timeout, a side effect that takes too long is cancelled, and onTimeout runs instead:

sideEffects {
    add<HomeAction.RefreshRequested>(
        timeout = 10.seconds,
        onTimeout = { dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed) }
    ) {
        // ...
    }
}

docs.title: When the screen is closed
docs.text:
When the screen is closed, the running side effects are cancelled, because nobody would see their result. Two options let work finish anyway, up to the closeTimeout of the configuration:

  • survivesClose = true: the side effect can finish after the screen is closed, like a request that saves what the user did.
  • onClose { }: work that starts when the screen is closed, like sending a result to the previous screen.
sideEffects {
    add<EditorAction.SaveClicked>(survivesClose = true) { saveDraftUseCase(state.draft) }
    onClose { broadcast(EditorBroadcast.Closed(state.draft)) }
}

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
If a side effect throws an exception, the error policy of the configuration decides: fail at once while developing, or report it and keep the screen working. For the errors you expect, like a failed request, return a result from the use case and dispatch an action, as in the examples above.

The errors and the side effect listener identify each side effect by the type of its action, RefreshRequested in the examples above. Pass name to add to choose another one: add<HomeAction.RefreshRequested>(name = "refreshFriends") { ... }.

docs.title: Side effects as values
docs.text:
A side effect can also be created with sideEffectOf, or written as a class that implements SideEffect, to declare it as a property, share it or receive it in the constructor. That is how the same screen can call the real backend in production and a mock in a demo build:

class HomeViewModel(private val getFriendsUseCase: GetFriendsUseCase) :
    EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(HomeState()) {

    private val openFriend = sideEffectOf(HomeAction.FriendClicked::class) { action ->
        publish(HomeEvent.FriendSelected(action.friend))
    }

    override fun setup() = source {
        sideEffects { add(openFriend) }
    }
}

See Pieces are values and Dependency injection and environments.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Keep the business logic in use cases. The side effect calls them and turns their result into actions.
  • Dispatch an action for each step of the work, like Started, Loaded and Failed in your first side effect. Then the reducers can show each step (loading, list, error), and the tests can check it too.
  • Choose the concurrency on purpose. Every is the default, but most user actions want Leading or Latest.

docs.title: EmaSource
docs.text:
An EmaSource is the engine of Emanate: it holds a state, receives actions and runs the middlewares, reducers and side effects that handle them. Every EmaViewModel has one inside.

Most apps only need ViewModels. An EmaSource is for the cases where you want that same engine without a screen: a state that several screens share, or logic that has nothing to do with the UI. It can also be the base of a custom ViewModel built from scratch, when the behavior of a standard EmaViewModel doesn't fit what you need.

docs.title: ViewModel or EmaSource?
docs.text:
An EmaSource has the same pieces as a ViewModel. What changes is everything around them:

EmaViewModel EmaSource Middlewares, reducers, side effects, broadcasts, plugins Yes Yes Who creates it Its screen, once You The initializer and the lifecycle, as actions Yes No: it only receives the actions you send it Logs of every action Automatic If you add them When it is closed When its screen is closed When you call close() Use it for A screen A state that is not a screen, or a custom ViewModel built from scratch

Use an EmaSource when the state doesn't belong to one screen, for example:

  • A shopping cart that the product screens fill and the checkout screen shows.
  • A music player that keeps playing while the user moves between screens.
  • A queue of downloads that runs in the background.
  • A ViewModel of your own: wrap an EmaSource in your class and expose only what your screen needs, without the lifecycle of an EmaViewModel.

docs.title: Creating an EmaSource
docs.text:
Create it with EmaSource(...): the initial state, and the same blocks as the setup of a ViewModel.

data class CartState(val products: List<Product> = emptyList()) : EmaState {
    val total get() = products.sumOf { it.price }
}

sealed interface CartAction : EmaAction {
    data class ProductAdded(val product: Product) : CartAction
    data class ProductRemoved(val product: Product) : CartAction
}

fun cartSource() = EmaSource<CartState, CartAction, EmaEvent.EMPTY>(CartState()) {
    reducers {
        add<CartAction> { action ->
            when (action) {
                is CartAction.ProductAdded -> state.copy(products = state.products + action.product)
                is CartAction.ProductRemoved -> state.copy(products = state.products - action.product)
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
To Call Send an action cart.dispatch(CartAction.ProductAdded(product)) Read the current state cart.state Follow the state cart.stateFlow.collect { state -> ... } Follow the events cart.eventFlow, and cart.consumeEvent(event) once each one is handled Stop it cart.close()

close() processes the actions still pending and then cancels the work of the EmaSource. An EmaSource has no screen that closes it, so close it yourself when it isn't needed anymore. An EmaSource created once for the whole app, like the cart, can live as long as the app.

docs.title: Example: a cart shared by two screens
docs.text:
The cart is created once, for example as a single of your dependency injection, and the ViewModels of two screens receive it in their constructor:

The product screen sends actions to the cart from a side effect:

class ProductViewModel(private val cart: EmaSource<CartState, CartAction, EmaEvent.EMPTY>) :
    EmaViewModel<ProductState, ProductAction, ProductEvent>(ProductState()) {

    override fun setup() = source {
        sideEffects {
            add<ProductAction.AddClicked> { cart.dispatch(CartAction.ProductAdded(state.product)) }
        }
    }
}

The checkout screen follows the state of the cart, and turns every change into an action of its own:

class CheckoutViewModel(private val cart: EmaSource<CartState, CartAction, EmaEvent.EMPTY>) :
    EmaViewModel<CheckoutState, CheckoutAction, CheckoutEvent>(CheckoutState()) {

    override fun setup() = source {
        reducers {
            add<CheckoutAction.CartChanged> { action -> state.copy(total = action.total) }
        }
        sideEffects {
            // Runs while the screen exists: it is cancelled when the ViewModel is closed
            add<EmaInitializer> {
                cart.stateFlow.collect { cart -> dispatch(CheckoutAction.CartChanged(cart.total)) }
            }
        }
    }
}

Each screen keeps its own state, and the cart is the only place where the products are.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
A ViewModel logs every action by itself, but an EmaSource doesn't. To see its actions with the state before and after them, add loggerMiddleware as its last middleware:

fun cartSource() = EmaSource<CartState, CartAction, EmaEvent.EMPTY>(CartState()) {
    middlewares(MiddlewarePosition.Last) {
        add(loggerMiddleware(tag = "Cart", logger = EmaLogger.Println))
    }
    // ...
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
An EmaSource uses the configuration of the application (the one set with Emanate.init), like a ViewModel does. To give one EmaSource its own, pass it as the second parameter:

EmaSource<CartState, CartAction, EmaEvent.EMPTY>(CartState(), configuration) { ... }

That configuration decides, among other things, the dispatcher where the EmaSource runs (main by default) and what happens when an exception is thrown.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
emanate-test works with an EmaSource like with a ViewModel. Call useTestConfiguration() before creating the EmaSource, so it runs on the dispatcher of the test. Then call record() on the EmaSource before sending the first action, and the recorder keeps every action, state and event in order, so you can assert on them. For example, a test of the cart above could look like this:

val recorder = cart.record()

cart.dispatch(CartAction.ProductAdded(product))

recorder.assertState { it.products == listOf(product) }

docs.title: State
docs.text:
The state is an immutable data class with everything the screen needs to draw itself.

data class HomeState(
    val user: User? = null,
    val query: String = STRING_EMPTY,
    val friends: List<User> = emptyList(),
    val isLoading: Boolean = false,
    val errorQueryTooShort: Boolean = false,
    val dialog: HomeDialog? = null
) : EmaState

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Make it a data class. copy is how the next state is created, and its equals lets the view skip states that did not change. Use EmaState.EMPTY for screens with no state.
  • Make it immutable. Use val and read-only collections. Change it with copy.
  • Give it default values (or a DEFAULT instance). They become the initial state and are handy for previews and tests.
  • Add derived properties instead of duplicating data. They keep the view free of logic:
data class HomeState(
    val user: User? = null,
    val friends: List<User> = emptyList(),
    // ...
) : EmaState {

    val showCreateButton get() = user?.role == Role.ADMIN
    val showEmptyList get() = user != null && friends.isEmpty()
}

docs.title: Changing the state
docs.text:
The state only changes in the reducers of the ViewModel, which return the next state with copy:

reducers {
    add<HomeAction> { action ->
        when (action) {
            is HomeAction.QueryWritten -> state.copy(query = action.query, errorQueryTooShort = false)
            // ...
        }
    }
}

The middlewares and side effects can read the current value with state, but never change it:

sideEffects {
    add<HomeAction.RefreshRequested> {
        if (state.isLoading) return@add
        // ...
    }
}

The state is exposed as stateFlow: StateFlow<S>. Because it is a StateFlow, equal consecutive states are not delivered twice and slow collectors only see the latest value.

docs.title: Modelling dialogs, loading and errors
docs.text:
Emanate does not have special "loading" or "error" states. They are ordinary fields of your state, so they survive a configuration change and are easy to test.

A dialog: a nullable sealed type. null means no dialog.

sealed interface HomeDialog {
    data object LoadError : HomeDialog
}

// Reducers
is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed -> state.copy(isLoading = false, dialog = HomeDialog.LoadError)  // show
is HomeAction.ErrorAccepted -> state.copy(dialog = null)                                    // hide

Loading: a boolean, set by the action that starts the work and cleared by the one that reports its result.

is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted -> state.copy(isLoading = true)
is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded -> state.copy(isLoading = false, friends = action.friends)

Field errors: one boolean (or a message) per field, named with the prefix error. Set it when the input is not valid, and clear it when the user edits the field:

// Reducers
is HomeAction.RefreshRequested -> state.copy(errorQueryTooShort = state.query.length == 1)  // show
is HomeAction.QueryWritten -> state.copy(query = action.query, errorQueryTooShort = false)  // hide

The view only draws what the field says:

@Composable
override fun onState(state: HomeState, actions: EmaActionDispatcher<HomeAction>) {
    OutlinedTextField(
        value = state.query,
        onValueChange = { query -> actions.dispatch(HomeAction.QueryWritten(query)) },
        isError = state.errorQueryTooShort,
        supportingText = {
            if (state.errorQueryTooShort) Text(text = "Write at least two letters")
        }
    )
}

docs.title: Rendering the state
docs.text: The view simply draws the state it receives. With Compose, recomposition does the diffing. See Compose screens.

docs.title: What does not belong in the state
docs.text:
• One-shot things: messages, navigation. Use events.
  • Platform types, like a context, a view or an image of the platform. Use EmaText for texts with resources, see Texts in the state.
  • Mutable collections or objects that change without you calling copy.

docs.title: ViewModel
docs.text:
An EmaViewModel is the logic of a screen. The view only draws and tells what the user does; the ViewModel decides everything else. That is where all the pieces described in the previous pages come together: the state, the actions, the events, and the reducers, side effects, middlewares, broadcasts and plugins that handle them.

The conversation between the two always has the same shape:

  • The view sends actions: what the user does, like writing in the search field or pulling to refresh, and the lifecycle of the screen.
  • The ViewModel sends back the state: everything the screen draws. Each time it changes, the view draws it again.
  • And the events: what happens once, like navigating to the detail of a friend.

Each screen has its own ViewModel. It is a plain Kotlin class, with no platform code, so it can be tested and shared between platforms.

docs.title: Your first ViewModel, in three steps
docs.text:
1. Extend EmaViewModel with the three types of the screen, and pass the initial state:

class HomeViewModel(
    private val getFriendsUseCase: GetFriendsUseCase,
    initialState: HomeState = HomeState()
) : EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(initialState)

2. Declare its pieces in setup. It returns source { }, where each kind of piece has its own block:

class HomeViewModel(
    private val getFriendsUseCase: GetFriendsUseCase,
    initialState: HomeState = HomeState()
) : EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(initialState) {

    override fun setup() = source {
        reducers {
            add<HomeAction> { action ->
                when (action) {
                    is HomeAction.QueryWritten -> state.copy(query = action.query)
                    is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted -> state.copy(isLoading = true)
                    is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded -> state.copy(isLoading = false, friends = action.friends)
                    is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed -> state.copy(isLoading = false, dialog = HomeDialog.LoadError)
                    is HomeAction.RefreshRequested,
                    is HomeAction.FriendClicked -> state
                }
            }
        }
        sideEffects {
            add<HomeAction.RefreshRequested>(concurrency = SideEffectConcurrency.Leading) {
                dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted)
                getFriendsUseCase(GetFriendsUseCase.Input(state.query))
                    .onSuccess { friends -> dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded(friends)) }
                    .onFailure { dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed) }
            }
            add<HomeAction.FriendClicked> { action ->
                publish(HomeEvent.FriendSelected(action.friend))
            }
        }
    }
}

3. Give it to the screen. The screen creates it once, and keeps it while the screen exists:

emaScreen(
    screenContent = HomeScreenContent(),
    viewModel = { HomeViewModel(getFriendsUseCase) },
    onEvent = { event -> /* navigation */ }
)

That's all: the screen draws the state, sends the actions and handles the events. See Compose screens and Dependency injection.

docs.title: What happens when the user does something
docs.text:
Every action takes the same path: middlewares, reducers, side effects. The reducers return the new state, and the view draws it. When a side effect dispatches an action, that action starts the path again from the beginning.

This is a refresh in the ViewModel above. Each row is one action:

  1. The view sends RefreshRequested. The reducers leave the state as it is, and the side effect loadFriends starts.
  2. The side effect dispatches Started. It goes through the middlewares, and a reducer returns isLoading = true: the view shows the loader.
  3. The side effect calls the use case and waits. The screen keeps working meanwhile.
  4. When the friends arrive, it dispatches Loaded(friends). Same path: a reducer puts them in the state, and the view draws the list.

This ViewModel has no middlewares, so each action goes straight on, as if a middleware called next().

docs.title: The setup
docs.text:
setup is where the ViewModel declares its pieces. Each kind has its own block:

Block Adds middlewares { } Middlewares: they decide the path of an action before anything else. reducers { } Reducers: they return the next state. sideEffects { } Side effects: they run the work that an action starts. broadcasts { listen<T>() } Broadcasts: the actions of other screens that it receives. plugins { } Plugins: groups of pieces reused in many screens.

A few rules apply to all of them:

  • add<Type> { } creates a piece for the actions of that type, and add(piece) installs a piece that already exists, like a property of the ViewModel or a plugin. add accepts several pieces, add(first, second), or a collection, add(pieces). Two pieces of the same kind can also be joined with first + second, which gives a list that add accepts.
  • The pieces of the same kind run in the order they are added. A block can be used more than once: its pieces go after the ones of the previous blocks of the same kind.
  • setup runs once, the first time the ViewModel is used, not in its constructor. So it can use the properties of the class, like its use cases.

docs.title: Pieces are values
docs.text:
A piece doesn't have to be written inside setup. It can be a property of the ViewModel, declared with reducerOf or sideEffectOf, and installed with add:

class HomeViewModel(
    private val getFriendsUseCase: GetFriendsUseCase,
    initialState: HomeState = HomeState()
) : EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(initialState) {

    private val homeReducer = reducerOf(HomeAction::class) { action ->
        when (action) {
            is HomeAction.QueryWritten -> state.copy(query = action.query)
            is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted -> state.copy(isLoading = true)
            is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded -> state.copy(isLoading = false, friends = action.friends)
            is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed -> state.copy(isLoading = false, dialog = HomeDialog.LoadError)
            is HomeAction.RefreshRequested,
            is HomeAction.FriendClicked -> state
        }
    }

    private val refresh = sideEffectOf(
        HomeAction.RefreshRequested::class,
        concurrency = SideEffectConcurrency.Leading
    ) {
        dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted)
        getFriendsUseCase(GetFriendsUseCase.Input(state.query))
            .onSuccess { friends -> dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded(friends)) }
            .onFailure { dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed) }
    }

    private val openFriend = sideEffectOf(HomeAction.FriendClicked::class) { action ->
        publish(HomeEvent.FriendSelected(action.friend))
    }

    override fun setup() = source {
        reducers { add(homeReducer) }
        sideEffects {
            add(refresh, openFriend)
        }
    }
}

The setup only installs them. That is what lets a ViewModel receive a piece in its constructor, without knowing which implementation it gets: the same screen can call the real backend in production, use a mock in a demo build and a fake in the tests. See Dependency injection and environments.

docs.title: The lifecycle as actions
docs.text:
The EmaViewModel also receives the lifecycle states and the initialization data as actions. The same pieces that handle the user actions can handle these ones too.

Action When EmaInitializer Once, the first time the screen is created: its initializer, or EmaInitializer.EMPTY. EmaLifecycle.Started The screen becomes visible. EmaLifecycle.Resumed The screen is in the foreground. EmaLifecycle.Paused The screen is no longer fully visible. EmaLifecycle.Stopped The screen goes to the background. EmaLifecycle.Destroyed The last action, right before the ViewModel is closed.

The initializer arrives once, so recreating the screen doesn't receive it again. A reducer can change the state when these actions arrive, and a side effect can react to them:

override fun setup() = source {
    reducers {
        // The initializer gives the screen its first state
        add<HomeInitializer> { initializer ->
            when (initializer) {
                is HomeInitializer.HomeUser -> state.copy(user = initializer.user)
            }
        }
        // The dialog is closed when the user leaves the screen
        add<EmaLifecycle.Stopped> { state.copy(dialog = null) }
    }
    sideEffects {
        // The friends are loaded once, when the screen is created
        add<HomeInitializer> { dispatch(HomeAction.RefreshRequested) }
        // And refreshed every time the user comes back to the screen
        add<EmaLifecycle.Resumed> { dispatch(HomeAction.RefreshRequested) }
    }
}

For example, work that only makes sense while the user sees the screen, like a timer or location updates, starts with Started and stops with Stopped.

docs.title: When the ViewModel is closed
docs.text: After Destroyed, the ViewModel is closed and the work still running is cancelled, unless it is allowed to finish. See When the screen is closed.

docs.title: The ViewModel and its screen
docs.text:
One ViewModel per screen. The screen creates it the first time it is opened, with the viewModel function you give it, and keeps it while the screen exists. Recreating the view or coming back to the screen reuses it. When the screen is closed for good, the ViewModel receives Destroyed and is closed. Opening the screen again creates a new one.

emaScreen(
    screenContent = HomeScreenContent(),
    // Called once, the first time the screen is opened
    viewModel = { HomeViewModel(getFriendsUseCase) },
    onEvent = { event -> /* navigation */ }
)

docs.title: Drawing before the first change
docs.text:
By default the screen draws the initial state at once. To avoid a flash of empty content, override updateOnInitialization with false: the screen waits until the ViewModel receives its first action of the screen, or an initializer other than EmaInitializer.EMPTY.

class HomeViewModel(
    private val getFriendsUseCase: GetFriendsUseCase,
    initialState: HomeState = HomeState()
) : EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(initialState) {

    override val updateOnInitialization = false

    // ...
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The constructor also receives the configuration of the ViewModel: by default the one set with Emanate.init. It decides where the ViewModel runs and what happens with its errors. See Configuration.

class HomeViewModel(
    private val getFriendsUseCase: GetFriendsUseCase,
    initialState: HomeState = HomeState()
) : EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(
    initialState,
    configuration = EmaConfiguration.Android(debug = BuildConfig.DEBUG)
) {

    // ...
}

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Every EmaViewModel logs each action it receives, with the state before and after it. By default the logs go to the standard output, with the name of the ViewModel as tag. A block like this is shown for each action (abbreviated):

EMA_HomeViewModel: ********************** STARTING EMA ACTION LOGGING **********************
EMA_HomeViewModel: | Dispatched action
EMA_HomeViewModel: | QueryWritten(query=ana)
EMA_HomeViewModel: | State before apply action
EMA_HomeViewModel: | HomeState(query=, isLoading=false, friends=[])
EMA_HomeViewModel: | State after apply action
EMA_HomeViewModel: | HomeState(query=ana, isLoading=false, friends=[])
EMA_HomeViewModel: ********************** FINISHED EMA ACTION LOGGING **********************

The logger of the configuration decides where the logs go. To send them to your own logger, implement EmaLogger in the configuration:

Emanate.init(
    EmaConfiguration.Android(debug = BuildConfig.DEBUG).copy(
        logger = EmaLogger { tag, message -> Timber.tag(tag).d(message) }
    )
)

docs.title: Under the hood: EmaSource
docs.text:
Inside every EmaViewModel there is an EmaSource: the engine that runs the pieces. The source { } of setup is what builds it. The ViewModel adds what a screen needs on top of it: the lifecycle and the initializer as actions, the logs, and a life tied to its screen.

You don't need to know more to write screens. If you need the same engine without a screen, for example for a state shared by several screens, see EmaSource.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Emanate has a configuration for the whole application, set once, when it starts, with Emanate.init:

class MyApplication : Application() {

    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        Emanate.init(EmaConfiguration.Android(debug = BuildConfig.DEBUG))
    }
}
  • Call it before any ViewModel is created: ViewModels read the configuration when they are built.
  • It can be called only once. A second call throws IllegalStateException.
  • If it is never called, the default EmaConfiguration() is used. That is the usual case in unit tests and in non-Android platforms.

Register the application in AndroidManifest.xml (android:name=".MyApplication"). A ViewModel or an EmaSource can also receive its own configuration, which is used instead of the one of the application. See Explicit configuration.

docs.title: What can be configured
docs.text:
Each property configures one thing. The ones that hold an object with several parameters list them in their own column, before what the property configures.

Property Default EmaConfiguration() Parameters What it configures dispatchers EmaDispatchers() main: where ViewModels and EmaSource run, and so their reducers and side effects. Default Dispatchers.Main.io: where use cases run, for network, disk and blocking work. Default Dispatchers.IO.default: CPU-intensive work, like processing images. Default Dispatchers.Default. The coroutine dispatchers. See Dispatchers. errorPolicy EmaErrorPolicy.Catch() Catch(onError): the exception is caught and the screen keeps working. onError is optional and receives each EmaError, to send it to a crash reporter.Throw: the exception is thrown again and the app fails at once. What happens when a middleware, reducer or side effect throws an exception. See Errors. logger EmaLogger.Println log(tag, message): writes one line. The tag is the name of the ViewModel.prefix: text added before every tag, to filter the logs of Emanate, like EMA_HomeViewModel. Set it with EmaLogger(prefix) { tag, message -> ... }. Where the logs go. null disables them. See Logs. printer EmaDataClassPrinter.ToString print(value): returns the text of the state or the action. By default its toString().indent and wrappedLineWidth: only in EmaAndroidDataClassPrinter. The spaces of each nesting level (2) and the length from which a long String is split into lines (80). How the states and actions are turned into text in the logs. See Printing the state. closeTimeout 5 seconds How long the work of a closed ViewModel can still run before it is cancelled. See Closing a ViewModel. sideEffectListener null onSuccess(reflection, output, duration): it finished without error. Receives its Reflection, what it launched (output) and how long it took.onError(error, duration): it threw an exception. Receives the EmaError and how long it took.onFinish(reflection, duration): it ended, with success, with error or cancelled. Receives every side effect that ends, to track or measure it. See Measuring the side effects. broadcaster EmaActionBroadcaster.Shared Shared: used by the whole process, so every ViewModel receives the actions broadcast by the others.EmaActionBroadcaster(): a new one isolates the ViewModels that use it, for example the ones of a library. Delivers the actions broadcast between ViewModels. See Libraries and SDKs.

docs.title: Configuration for Android
docs.text:
EmaConfiguration.Android(debug) is a predefined configuration in emanate-android (com.carmabs.emanate.android.configuration.Android). It is the one to use in an Android application, with BuildConfig.DEBUG as the flag. It changes these properties from the default configuration. Each column says the value that the property has, so you can compare them:

Property EmaConfiguration() Android(debug = true) Android(debug = false) errorPolicy Catch() Throw Catch() logger EmaLogger.Println EmaLogger.Logcat null dispatchers.main Dispatchers.Main Dispatchers.Main.immediate Dispatchers.Main.immediate printer EmaDataClassPrinter.ToString EmaAndroidDataClassPrinter() EmaAndroidDataClassPrinter()
