  • errorPolicy. With Throw, an exception in a middleware, reducer or side effect crashes the app at once, so you notice it while developing. With Catch(), it is caught and the screen keeps working. See Errors.
  • logger. In debug builds every action and state is written to logcat with Log.d. In release builds nothing is logged, so the state of the user, which may have personal data, never reaches logcat. See Logs.
  • dispatchers.main. Dispatchers.Main.immediate is what the viewModelScope of Android uses: the work started from the main thread, like dispatching an action from a click, runs at once instead of waiting for the next frame.
  • printer. EmaAndroidDataClassPrinter prints every field, indented. In release builds there is no logger, so it isn't used. See Printing the state.

Only errorPolicy and logger depend on the flag. closeTimeout, sideEffectListener, broadcaster and the other dispatchers keep the default values in all of them.

EmaConfiguration is a data class, so change only what you need with copy:

Emanate.init(
    EmaConfiguration.Android(debug = BuildConfig.DEBUG).copy(
        closeTimeout = 10.seconds
    )
)

docs.title: Dispatchers
docs.text:
EmaDispatchers groups the three coroutine dispatchers that Emanate uses, one for each kind of work. It is the dispatchers property of the configuration, and each one is applied in a different place:

Dispatcher Default Where it is applied main Dispatchers.Main The scope of every EmaViewModel and EmaSource. Everything the ViewModel does runs there: its middlewares, its reducers, its side effects and the dispatch of its actions. io Dispatchers.IO The use cases: EmaUseCase and EmaFlowUseCase switch to it to run, so the side effect that calls them doesn't block main. default Dispatchers.Default The CPU-intensive work of emanate-android: the extensions that create bitmaps from a ByteArray or a drawable resource (toBitmap, getBitmapFromResource, getBitmapCropFromResource), and the coroutines of EmaJobService.

main is the one you will change most. A side effect runs on main, so it can read the state and dispatch actions safely, and the work that blocks is delegated to a use case, which switches to io itself:

sideEffects {
    add<HomeAction.RefreshRequested> {
        // Runs on main
        dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted)
        // The use case switches to io, and comes back to main with the result
        getFriendsUseCase(GetFriendsUseCase.Input(state.query))
            .onSuccess { friends -> dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded(friends)) }
    }
}

In the tests, replace main with the dispatcher of the test, see Testing.

io is read by the use case when it is created, from Emanate.configuration, not from the configuration of the ViewModel that calls it. To use another one, for example the io of a library, pass it to the constructor of the use case.

default is read from Emanate.configuration when the work runs. You can use it for your own CPU-intensive work, so it is replaced together with the others in the tests:

suspend fun sortContacts(contacts: List<Contact>) =
    withContext(Emanate.configuration.dispatchers.default) { contacts.sortedBy { it.name } }

EmaConfiguration.Android(debug) only changes main, see Configuration for Android. Change any of them with copy, keeping the others:

val android = EmaConfiguration.Android(debug = BuildConfig.DEBUG)
Emanate.init(android.copy(dispatchers = android.dispatchers.copy(io = myIoDispatcher)))

docs.title: Printing the state
docs.text:
The logs print each state and action with the printer of the configuration. Take this state:

data class HomeState(
    val query: String = "",
    val isLoading: Boolean = false,
    val friends: List<User> = emptyList()
) : EmaState

With the default printer, EmaDataClassPrinter.ToString, it is its toString(), in a single line:

HomeState(query=An, isLoading=false, friends=[User(name=Ana, role=USER), User(name=Andrés, role=ADMIN)])

EmaConfiguration.Android(debug) uses EmaAndroidDataClassPrinter, which reads the fields and indents the nested objects, collections and maps, so a big state can be read at a glance:

HomeState(
  query = "An"
  isLoading = false
  friends = [
              User(
                name = "Ana"
                role = Role.USER
              ),
              User(
                name = "Andrés"
                role = Role.ADMIN
              )
            ]
)

It reads the fields with Java reflection, so it is only available on Android and the JVM. Change its indentation or the width where long texts are split with EmaAndroidDataClassPrinter(indent = 4, wrappedLineWidth = 120).

docs.title: A custom printer
docs.text:
Implement EmaDataClassPrinter to print the states your way. A useful case is hiding sensitive data, so it doesn't reach the logs of a QA build:

val maskedPrinter = EmaDataClassPrinter { value ->
    value.toString()
        .replace(Regex("(password|token)=[^,)]*"), "$1=***")
}

Emanate.init(EmaConfiguration.Android(debug = BuildConfig.DEBUG).copy(printer = maskedPrinter))

LoginState(user=ana, password=***, isLoading=false)

To print any object with the printer of the configuration, use toStringPretty().

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Emanate writes its logs with the logger of the configuration. A logger is a function that receives a tag, the name of the ViewModel, and a message:

Logger Where it writes Used by EmaLogger.Println The standard output, with EMA_ before the tag. EmaConfiguration() EmaLogger.Logcat Logcat with Log.d, with EMA_ before the tag. EmaConfiguration.Android(true) null Nowhere. EmaConfiguration.Android(false) Your own EmaLogger Wherever you want. Anything

Every EmaViewModel logs its actions with its name as tag:

  • One line when an action is received, before the middlewares. It shows the actions that a middleware stops, which don't reach the reducers.
  • A block with the action and the state before and after its reducers. It is written right before them, after all the middlewares, so the state after the action is correct even if a middleware continues it later with nextAfter, and the action is the one the reducers receive.

For the action QueryWritten("An") of the state above, logcat shows (the tag, EMA_HomeViewModel, is omitted):

Received action: QueryWritten(query=An)

**********************    STARTING EMA ACTION LOGGING    ***********************
**                                                                            **
|||||||||||||||||||||||||||    Dispatched action    ||||||||||||||||||||||||||||
||                                                                            ||
||    QueryWritten(query=An)                                                  ||
|||||||||||||||||||||||    State before apply action    ||||||||||||||||||||||||
||                                                                            ||
||    HomeState(                                                              ||
||      query = ""                                                            ||
||      isLoading = false                                                     ||
||      friends = []                                                          ||
||    )                                                                       ||
||||||||||||||||||||||||    State after apply action    ||||||||||||||||||||||||
||                                                                            ||
||    HomeState(                                                              ||
||      query = "An"                                                          ||
||      isLoading = false                                                     ||
||      friends = []                                                          ||
||    )                                                                       ||
||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||
**                                                                            **
**********************    FINISHED EMA ACTION LOGGING    ***********************

The errors caught by the error policy are logged too, with the same tag.

The state may contain data of the user, so don't log in release builds, as EmaConfiguration.Android(debug) does.

docs.title: A custom logger
docs.text:
An EmaLogger is a lambda, so it can send the logs wherever you need. To use Timber in debug builds:

Emanate.init(
    EmaConfiguration.Android(debug = BuildConfig.DEBUG).copy(
        logger = if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) EmaLogger { tag, message -> Timber.tag(tag).d(message) } else null
    )
)

Or keep the last actions as breadcrumbs of a crash report, and skip the big blocks of state:

val breadcrumbs = EmaLogger { tag, message ->
    // "Received action: ..." is one line and enough to know what the user did before the crash
    if (message.startsWith("Received action")) FirebaseCrashlytics.getInstance().log("$tag: $message")
}

Use EmaLogger(prefix = "MYAPP_") { tag, message -> ... } to add a prefix to every tag, so they can be filtered in logcat.

To disable the logs of a single ViewModel, pass it a configuration without logger: Emanate.configuration.copy(logger = null). An EmaSource used on its own doesn't log: add loggerMiddleware(tag, logger) as its last middleware.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
The code of your ViewModel can fail: a reducer that calls friends.first() on an empty list, a middleware that parses a wrong value, a side effect that throws. What Emanate does then is the errorPolicy.

Errors you expect are not exceptions. A request that can fail is not an error of this kind: return an EmaResult from the use case and let the side effect dispatch an action that shows the failure. The policy is for the bugs, the things you didn't expect.

Take a reducer with a bug:

reducers {
    add<HomeAction.FriendClicked> { action ->
        // Bug: throws NoSuchElementException when the friend isn't in the list
        state.copy(selected = state.friends.first { it.id == action.id })
    }
}
Throw Catch What happens The exception is thrown again where it happened, so the app crashes with its stack trace. The exception is caught. The app keeps running. The screen Closed by the crash. Still working. The state is the one it had before the action. The log The crash of the app. One line with the stack trace: HomeViewModel: action FriendClicked failed: java.util.NoSuchElementException ... onError Not called. Called with an EmaError. Use it While developing, so the bug can't go unnoticed. It is the default of EmaConfiguration.Android(true). In production, so a bug in one action doesn't take the whole app down. It is the default of EmaConfiguration() and of release builds.

What "keeps working" means depends on the piece that failed:

It threw in... With Catch A reducer The action is discarded: the state doesn't change and the next actions are processed as usual. A middleware The action is discarded and doesn't reach the reducers or the side effects. A side effect That side effect ends. The rest of the side effects and the actions keep working.

Cancellations are never errors: a side effect cancelled by its concurrency, its timeout or the closing of the ViewModel is not reported.

docs.title: Reporting the errors
docs.text:
With Catch, pass onError to send each error to your crash reporter, so a bug that is silent for the user is not silent for you:

Emanate.init(
    EmaConfiguration.Android(debug = BuildConfig.DEBUG).copy(
        errorPolicy = if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) {
            EmaErrorPolicy.Throw
        } else {
            EmaErrorPolicy.Catch { error ->
                crashReporter.recordException(error.exception)
                crashReporter.setCustomKey("viewModel", error.reflection.containerClassName)
                crashReporter.setCustomKey("where", error.reflection.name)
            }
        }
    )
)

An EmaError has:

Field Example exception The NoSuchElementException that was thrown. reflection.containerClassName HomeViewModel reflection.containerClassQualifiedName com.carmabs.sample.home.HomeViewModel reflection.name action FriendClicked for a middleware or a reducer. For a side effect, its name: RefreshRequested, see Naming the side effects.

To crash also in the QA builds, so the testers report the bugs instead of the app hiding them, use Throw there: the debug flag is only the default of EmaConfiguration.Android, and the policy is yours to choose.

docs.title: Measuring the side effects
docs.text:
To track the side effects, for example to measure how long they take, count how many fail or send them to your analytics, set a sideEffectListener. It is called for every side effect of every ViewModel, and it has three functions, all optional. Each one receives the duration the side effect took:

Function Called when Receives onSuccess(reflection, output, duration) A side effect finishes without error. The reflection and its output: what it launched while it ran. onError(error, duration) A side effect throws, with Catch and with Throw (right before the app fails). An EmaError: the reflection and the exception. onFinish(reflection, duration) A side effect ends: after onSuccess, after onError, or when it is cancelled. The reflection.

A cancellation (a new action with Latest, a timeout, the closing of the ViewModel) is not an error, so it only calls onFinish. That is how you tell the three endings apart: onSuccess is a success, onError a failure, and an onFinish with neither before it is a cancellation.

The Reflection says which side effect it is:

Field Example containerClassName HomeViewModel containerClassQualifiedName com.carmabs.sample.home.HomeViewModel name The name of the side effect, see Naming the side effects.

The SideEffectOutput says what the side effect produced, in the order it happened:

Field What it has actions The actions it dispatched to its ViewModel with dispatch: Started, Loaded(friends)... broadcasts The actions it sent to other ViewModels with broadcast. events The events it published for the view with publish.

It only has what that execution launched, not what other side effects launched at the same time. With all of it you can track, for each side effect, which ViewModel launched it, its name, how long it took, how it ended and what it produced:

class SideEffectTracker(private val analytics: Analytics) : EmaSideEffectListener {

    override fun onSuccess(reflection: Reflection, output: SideEffectOutput, duration: Duration) {
        analytics.track(
            event = "side_effect_success",
            "name" to "${reflection.containerClassName}.${reflection.name}",
            "millis" to duration.inWholeMilliseconds.toString(),
            // Loaded(friends = [...]), Failed...
            "actions" to output.actions.joinToString { it::class.simpleName.toString() }
        )
    }

    override fun onError(error: EmaError, duration: Duration) {
        analytics.track(
            event = "side_effect_error",
            "viewModel" to error.reflection.containerClassName,
            "name" to error.reflection.name,
            "error" to error.exception::class.simpleName.toString(),
            "millis" to duration.inWholeMilliseconds.toString()
        )
    }

    override fun onFinish(reflection: Reflection, duration: Duration) {
        // Also called by the cancelled ones
    }
}

Emanate.init(
    EmaConfiguration.Android(debug = BuildConfig.DEBUG).copy(sideEffectListener = SideEffectTracker(analytics))
)
  • onSuccess and onError are for tracking, not for handling. The error is also handled by the error policy: onError of the listener tells you about that side effect and its time, while the onError of EmaErrorPolicy.Catch is the place to report bugs.
  • A side effect doesn't return a value: it reports with actions and events, so that is what output has. The output of the onClose blocks has what they launched too. Keep in mind that the actions can have the data of the user, like the friends of Loaded(friends): send their type, as in the example, if that data must not leave the app.
  • The duration is the time the side effect was running, including the delays and the suspensions. A side effect that ends by its timeout calls onSuccess after the time of the timeout.

docs.title: Naming the side effects
docs.text:
The name of the Reflection identifies the work in the errors and in the sideEffectListener. Emanate gives it a name from what it knows:

Work Name Example A side effect of the setup The type of the action that launches it, or the name you pass. RefreshRequested A nextAfter of a middleware nextAfter and the type of the action it received. nextAfter QueryWritten An onClose block onClose onClose A reducer or a middleware that fails (errors only) action and the type of the action. action FriendClicked 
sideEffects {
    add<HomeAction.RefreshRequested> { /* ... */ }                       // RefreshRequested
    add<HomeAction.FriendClicked>(name = "openProfile") { /* ... */ }    // openProfile
}

Pass name to add, to sideEffectOf or to the name property of a class that implements SideEffect, when the type of the action isn't a good name, for example when two side effects listen to the same action or to a base type like EmaAction.

docs.title: Closing a ViewModel
docs.text:
When a ViewModel is closed, its side effects are cancelled, so the work that was running stops. Two things can still run after it:

  • the onClose blocks of its EmaSource, which are the last thing the ViewModel does, and
  • the side effects added with survivesClose = true, like the one that saves a draft when the user leaves the editor.

The closeTimeout is how long they have. After it, they are cancelled, so a request that never answers doesn't keep the ViewModel alive for ever. By default it is 5 seconds.

sideEffects {
    add<EditorAction.SaveClicked>(survivesClose = true) { saveDraftUseCase(state.draft) }
}

If the user leaves the editor and the save takes 8 seconds, it is cancelled at the 5th. For slower work, increase it:

Emanate.init(EmaConfiguration.Android(debug = BuildConfig.DEBUG).copy(closeTimeout = 15.seconds))

Keep it short: it is the time a ViewModel that was already closed stays in memory. See Side effects.

docs.title: Explicit configuration
docs.text:
Emanate.configuration is shared by the whole process. EmaViewModel and EmaSource(...) read it when they are created, as the default value of their configuration parameter, which goes right after the initial state. Pass one to use it instead:

class HomeViewModel(
    private val getFriendsUseCase: GetFriendsUseCase,
    configuration: EmaConfiguration = Emanate.configuration
) : EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(HomeState(), configuration) {
    // ...
}

The ViewModel runs on its main dispatcher and logs with its logger. The configuration is kept by the ViewModel and its EmaSource, so its error policy, side effect listener, closeTimeout and broadcaster are the ones of the configuration they received.

Use Emanate.init in an application: it configures every ViewModel in one place, and they don't need any parameter. Pass the configuration when the one of the application isn't enough or can't be relied on:

  • Libraries and SDKs. Emanate.init can be called only once and belongs to the application. A library built with Emanate passes its own configuration to its ViewModels, so it doesn't clash with an application that also uses Emanate, nor depend on whether it was initialized. See Libraries and SDKs.
  • A module with a different configuration, for example its own logger or error policy.
  • Dependency injection. The configuration is one more dependency, provided by Koin or any other dependency injection framework. See Dependency injection.
  • Tests. Each test passes its configuration, with the dispatchers of the test, without changing the one of Emanate, so the tests can run in parallel. See Testing.

The use cases don't receive the whole configuration, only a dispatcher in the constructor: by default the io dispatcher of the configuration of Emanate, so pass the io dispatcher of yours.

docs.title: Libraries and SDKs
docs.text:
A library built with Emanate can be used by an application that also uses Emanate and calls Emanate.init. To keep them apart, the library doesn't call Emanate.init nor use the configuration of Emanate: it creates its own and passes it to all its pieces.

internal object MyLibraryEmanate {
    val configuration = EmaConfiguration.Android(debug = BuildConfig.DEBUG).copy(
        logger = if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) EmaLogger(prefix = "MYLIB_") { tag, message -> Log.d(tag, message) } else null,
        broadcaster = EmaActionBroadcaster()
    )
}

docs.title: Wrap the classes of Emanate in base classes
docs.text:
Passing the configuration in every ViewModel and use case of the library is easy to forget: one that doesn't receive it silently uses the one of the application, or the default one if the application never initialized Emanate. Don't extend the classes of Emanate directly in the library: create a base class for each one that already passes the configuration, and extend only those:

internal abstract class MyLibViewModel<S : EmaState, A : EmaAction, E : EmaEvent>(initialState: S) :
    EmaViewModel<S, A, E>(initialState, MyLibraryEmanate.configuration)

internal abstract class MyLibUseCase<I, O> :
    EmaUseCase<I, O>(MyLibraryEmanate.configuration.dispatchers.io)

internal abstract class MyLibFlowUseCase<I, O> :
    EmaFlowUseCase<I, O>(MyLibraryEmanate.configuration.dispatchers.io)

The classes of the library extend them, and there is nothing to remember:

internal class PayUseCase(private val repository: PaymentRepository) : MyLibUseCase<Payment, Receipt>() {
    // ...
}

internal class PaymentViewModel(private val payUseCase: PayUseCase) :
    MyLibViewModel<PaymentState, PaymentAction, PaymentEvent>(PaymentState()) {
    // ...
}

The base classes are also the place to add what every piece of the library shares, like a plugin that all its ViewModels install. If the library creates an EmaSource on its own with EmaSource(...), wrap it the same way.

  • Broadcast actions. With its own EmaActionBroadcaster, the ViewModels of the library only receive the actions broadcast by each other, and the ones of the application don't receive theirs. Keep the shared one, EmaActionBroadcaster.Shared, if the library and the application send results to each other.
  • Public ViewModels. If the application must create the ViewModels of the library, expose factories or a public base class of your own, not the classes of Emanate, so the configuration can't be skipped.

If the application must be able to change something, like the logger, add a function to the library that receives it before any of its screens is opened, instead of using Emanate.init.

The application and the library use the same emanate-core: the version that Gradle resolves for both. Keep the library on a version compatible with the applications that use it.

docs.title: Dependency injection and environments
docs.text:
Emanate does not depend on any dependency injection framework. Wherever it needs a ViewModel, it asks you for it with a function, so you can use Koin, a manual container or plain constructors.

emaScreen(
    screenContent = HomeScreenContent(),
    viewModel = { HomeViewModel(getFriendsUseCase, HomeState()) },
    onEvent = { /* ... */ }
)

And because the behaviour of a screen is a list of pieces (middlewares, reducers and side effects) that can be replaced, the same injection decides how the screen behaves: the real backend in production, mocked data in a development build, latency or errors in QA, a fake in the tests. The ViewModel, the screen and the rest of the app stay exactly the same.

docs.title: One ViewModel per screen
docs.text: Emanate calls the function once, when the screen is opened for the first time, and keeps the ViewModel while the screen exists: see How the ViewModel is kept alive. The function must create the ViewModel, not return one that already exists, so each screen gets its own. A singleton would be shared by every screen of that type and would keep the state of a screen that was already closed.

docs.title: With Koin
docs.text:
This is how the sample app does it. Start Koin after initializing Emanate:

class EmaSampleApplication : Application() {

    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        Emanate.init(EmaConfiguration.Android(debug = BuildConfig.DEBUG))
        startKoin {
            androidContext(this@EmaSampleApplication)
            modules(dataModule, useCaseModule, uiModule)
        }
    }
}

Repositories are usually singletons and use cases are created when needed. Declare the ViewModels as factory, so each screen gets its own. The initial state can be injected too, which keeps the default state in one place:

val dataModule = module {
    single<Repository> { RemoteRepository() }
}

val useCaseModule = module {
    factory { GetFriendsUseCase(get()) }
}

val uiModule = module {
    factoryOf(::HomeViewModel)
    factory { HomeState() }
}

emaScreen(
    screenContent = HomeScreenContent(),
    viewModel = { get<HomeViewModel>() },
    onEvent = { /* ... */ }
)

docs.title: The store of a backup
docs.text:
A ViewModel that survives the death of the process receives its EmaStateStore in the constructor. The function that creates the ViewModel receives the store of the screen, so pass it on. With Koin, as a parameter:

val uiModule = module {
    factory { (stateStore: EmaStateStore) -> HomeViewModel(get(), stateStore) }
}

emaScreen(
    screenContent = HomeScreenContent(),
    viewModel = { store -> get<HomeViewModel> { parametersOf(store) } },
    onEvent = { /* ... */ }
)

On the platforms without a store, or in a test that doesn't check the saved state, pass EmaStateStore.None.

docs.title: Injecting pieces
docs.text:
Besides use cases, a ViewModel can receive its middlewares, reducers and side effects. A ViewModel that receives a piece instead of declaring it doesn't know which one it gets.

The home screen loads the friends of the user. Take the side effect that loads them out of the ViewModel, as a class that implements SideEffect. A type alias keeps the signatures short:

typealias FriendsEffect = SideEffect<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent, HomeAction.RefreshRequested>

class LiveFriends(private val getFriendsUseCase: GetFriendsUseCase) : FriendsEffect {

    override val actionType = HomeAction.RefreshRequested::class
    override val concurrency = SideEffectConcurrency.Leading

    override suspend fun SideEffectScope<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>.invoke(action: HomeAction.RefreshRequested) {
        dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted)
        getFriendsUseCase(GetFriendsUseCase.Input(state.query))
            .onSuccess { friends -> dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded(friends)) }
            .onFailure { dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed) }
    }
}

The ViewModel receives it and installs it with add. Middlewares can be received the same way:

class HomeViewModel(
    private val loadFriends: FriendsEffect,
    private val tuning: List<EmaMiddleware<HomeState, HomeAction, *>> = emptyList(),
    initialState: HomeState = HomeState()
) : EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(initialState) {

    override fun setup() = source {
        // Before anything else, so they see every action first
        middlewares(MiddlewarePosition.First) {
            tuning.forEach { add(it) }
        }
        reducers {
            add<HomeAction> { action ->
                when (action) {
                    is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted -> state.copy(isLoading = true)
                    is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded -> state.copy(isLoading = false, friends = action.friends)
                    is HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed -> state.copy(isLoading = false, dialog = HomeDialog.LoadError)
                    // ...
                }
            }
        }
        sideEffects {
            add(loadFriends)
            add<HomeAction.FriendClicked> { action -> publish(HomeEvent.FriendSelected(action.friend)) }
        }
    }
}

A mock is one more implementation of the same piece. It dispatches the same actions as the real one, so the rest of the screen can't tell the difference:

class MockFriends(
    private val friends: List<User>?,
    private val latency: Duration = 500.milliseconds
) : FriendsEffect {

    override val actionType = HomeAction.RefreshRequested::class
    override val concurrency = SideEffectConcurrency.Leading

    override suspend fun SideEffectScope<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>.invoke(action: HomeAction.RefreshRequested) {
        dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted)
        delay(latency)
        dispatch(if (friends != null) HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded(friends) else HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed)
    }
}

MockFriends(friends = null) shows the error dialog, MockFriends(emptyList()) the empty list and MockFriends(hundredFriends) a long one. The reducers and the events don't change: the screen still shows its loading state, its error dialog and its navigation exactly as in production.

docs.title: Two behaviours by flavor on Android: dev and pro
docs.text:
This example is specific to Android, the only platform with product flavors. On the other platforms you get the same result by choosing the modules in each target, or with a manual factory.

Decide the pieces where the ViewModel is created: in the dependency injection of each build. With two Android flavors, dev works without a backend and pro calls the real one:

// build.gradle.kts of the app
android {
    flavorDimensions += "environment"
    productFlavors {
        create("dev") { dimension = "environment" }
        create("pro") { dimension = "environment" }
    }
}

The main source set declares what both builds share, and the source set of each flavor declares a module with the same name and its own pieces:

// src/main: the same in every build
val homeModule = module {
    factory {
        HomeViewModel(loadFriends = get(), tuning = get(named("homeTuning")), initialState = get())
    }
}

// src/pro: the real backend
val environmentModule = module {
    factory<FriendsEffect> { LiveFriends(get()) }
    factory<List<EmaMiddleware<HomeState, HomeAction, *>>>(named("homeTuning")) { emptyList() }
}

// src/dev: mocked friends and a slow network
val environmentModule = module {
    factory<FriendsEffect> { MockFriends(friends = demoFriends) }
    factory<List<EmaMiddleware<HomeState, HomeAction, *>>>(named("homeTuning")) {
        listOf(middlewareDelayOf(HomeAction.RefreshRequested::class, 2.seconds))
    }
}

startKoin {
    modules(dataModule, useCaseModule, homeModule, environmentModule)
}

Each build compiles only the environmentModule of its flavor, so the mocks never reach the pro build. The list of middlewares has a name because Koin can't tell two List types apart. The same works with build types (debug, qa, release), with any other dependency injection framework, or with a manual factory.

docs.title: The environments of the sample
docs.text:
The sample app applies this idea to its repositories, with three flavors. Each one has its own environmentModule in src/<flavor> that binds the two repositories, and an AppEnvironment that the login screen shows as a label in the corner, except in pro:

Flavor LoginRepository FriendsRepository For mock MockLoginRepository, instant InMemoryFriendsRepository with three friends, nothing saved Demos and working offline: it always starts the same dev MockLoginRepository, 2 seconds DelayedFriendsRepository over MapFriendsRepository Seeing the loading states and the animations of a slow network pro ApiLoginRepository over a LoginApi MapFriendsRepository The real path: the LoginApi is the piece a network client replaces 
// app/src/mock
val environmentModule = module {
    single { AppEnvironment("mock") }
    single<LoginRepository> { MockLoginRepository(latency = ZERO) }
    single<FriendsRepository> { InMemoryFriendsRepository(demoFriends) }
}

The use cases, the ViewModels and the screens are the same in the three builds. The repositories are named after the kind of implementation they are, not with an Impl suffix. Each implementation lives in the source set of the environment that uses it (MockLoginRepository in src/mockDev, shared by mock and dev), so the production build doesn't carry classes it doesn't use; the pro label tone is Invisible, so nothing is drawn there. Choose the variant in Build Variants of Android Studio, or with ./gradlew :app:assembleMockDebug. Each flavor has its own application id, so the three can be installed together.

docs.title: What an environment can change
docs.text: You replace exactly the behaviour you want to change, at the size you want: one response, one delay, one rule. Without Emanate, this usually means an if (isDemo) inside the ViewModel, a fake implementation of a whole repository, or a mocking library that only works in the tests.

docs.title: Latency
docs.text:
middlewareDelayOf delays the actions of a type before they reach the reducers and the side effects, to see every loading state as a slow network would show it:

val slowRefresh = middlewareDelayOf<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeAction.RefreshRequested>(
    HomeAction.RefreshRequested::class,
    2.seconds
)

With nextAfter, a middleware can also decide the delay, for example a random one for every action:

val randomLatency = middlewareOf<HomeState, HomeAction, EmaAction>(EmaAction::class) {
    nextAfter { delay(Random.nextLong(200, 1500)) }
}

docs.title: Errors and disabled features
docs.text:
A middleware can replace an action with next(action). This one turns every refresh into a failure, so the error dialog can be checked in a build that talks to the real backend:

val failingRefresh = middlewareOf<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeAction.RefreshRequested>(HomeAction.RefreshRequested::class) {
    next(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed)
}

And one that doesn't call next stops the action: it never reaches the reducers nor the side effects. For example, to keep a feature disabled in a build:

val profilesDisabled = middlewareOf<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeAction.FriendClicked>(HomeAction.FriendClicked::class) {
    // Not calling next: the profiles can't be opened in this build
}

docs.title: A different business rule
docs.text:
Reducers can be replaced too, to change a business rule in one build. A development build can give every user the administrator role, to show the screens that only administrators see, without a special account:

class HomeViewModel(
    private val userReducer: EmaReducer<HomeState, HomeInitializer> = reducerOf(HomeInitializer::class) { initializer ->
        when (initializer) {
            is HomeInitializer.HomeUser -> state.copy(user = initializer.user)
        }
    }
) : EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(HomeState()) {

    override fun setup() = source {
        reducers { add(userReducer) }
    }
}

// dev
HomeViewModel(
    userReducer = reducerOf(HomeInitializer::class) { initializer ->
        when (initializer) {
            is HomeInitializer.HomeUser -> state.copy(user = initializer.user.copy(role = Role.ADMIN))
        }
    }
)

docs.title: The starting state
docs.text:
For QA, open a screen already in the state you want to check, without repeating the steps that lead to it. Receive the initial state in the constructor, with the usual one as default, and pass the one you need:

class HomeViewModel(
    private val loadFriends: FriendsEffect,
    initialState: HomeState = HomeState()
) : EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(initialState) {
    // ...
}

// QA: a search with no results
HomeViewModel(
    loadFriends = MockFriends(friends = emptyList()),
    initialState = HomeState(query = "Zoe", friends = emptyList())
)

With the environment modules of the flavors, each build provides its own state and the homeModule of src/main passes it with initialState = get():

// src/pro
val environmentModule = module {
    factory { HomeState() }
}

// src/dev
val environmentModule = module {
    factory { HomeState(query = "Zoe", friends = emptyList()) }
}

The state is built by hand, so keep it a valid one.

docs.title: The tests
docs.text: The tests create the ViewModel with the pieces they need, with no mocking library and no device: HomeViewModel(loadFriends = MockFriends(friends = null)). See Testing.

docs.title: Injecting the configuration
docs.text:
By default the ViewModels use the configuration set with Emanate.init, so they don't need to receive it. To inject it instead, for example in a library that can't call Emanate.init or in a module with its own configuration, receive it in the constructor and pass it to the ViewModel. See Explicit configuration.

class HomeViewModel(
    private val getFriendsUseCase: GetFriendsUseCase,
    configuration: EmaConfiguration
) : EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(HomeState(), configuration)

With Koin, declare it as a single:

val uiModule = module {
    single { EmaConfiguration.Android(debug = BuildConfig.DEBUG) }
    factoryOf(::HomeViewModel)
}

The use cases only receive the io dispatcher of the configuration, in the constructor:

val useCaseModule = module {
    factory { GetFriendsUseCase(get(), get<EmaConfiguration>().dispatchers.io) }
}

docs.title: Guidelines
docs.text:
• Declare the ViewModel as factory. Each screen needs its own instance; a single would share the state of a screen that was already closed.
  • Inject the pieces, not the ViewModel, and only the ones that an environment may change. Receive in the constructor the side effect of the backend, the middlewares or the initial state, with the production ones as default values. What never changes stays inside the ViewModel, so the constructor doesn't grow with every detail.
  • Choose the environment in the dependency injection, never in the ViewModel. An if (isDemo) inside the ViewModel is a branch that production carries and nobody tests.
  • Keep the mocks out of the production build. Declare them in the source set of their flavor or build type, as in the flavors example.
  • Run the middlewares that simulate conditions first, with MiddlewarePosition.First, so they act before the middlewares of the screen.
  • Use a plugin for a whole feature that an environment installs or not, like analytics or a debug overlay. See Plugins.

docs.title: Initializers: passing data to a screen
docs.text: An initializer is the data a screen needs to start. It travels in the route of the destination and reaches the ViewModel as an action, once, the first time the screen is created.

docs.title: Declare it
docs.text:
@Serializable
sealed interface HomeInitializer : EmaInitializer {

    @Serializable
    data class HomeUser(val user: User) : HomeInitializer
}

A sealed type lets one screen start in different ways. A screen that receives nothing gets EmaInitializer.EMPTY.

docs.title: Use it in the ViewModel
docs.text:
The initializer is one more action: a reducer applies its data to the state, and a side effect loads what the screen needs.

override fun setup() = source {
    reducers {
        add<HomeInitializer> { initializer ->
            when (initializer) {
                is HomeInitializer.HomeUser -> state.copy(
                    userData = HomeState.UserData(initializer.user.name, initializer.user.surname, initializer.user.role)
                )
            }
        }
    }
    sideEffects {
        add<HomeInitializer> { initializer ->
            when (initializer) {
                is HomeInitializer.HomeUser -> dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.FriendsLoaded(getFriendsUseCase(Unit)))
            }
        }
    }
}

It arrives once, so a rotation doesn't apply it nor load the data again. After the death of the process, the screen receives it again, and a backup restores what the user typed on top of it.

docs.title: Send and receive it
docs.text:
The initializer travels as text inside the route, serialized with kotlinx.serialization: annotate it with @Serializable and any character is allowed in its values.

  • The screen that navigates sends it with NavController.navigate(route, initializerBundle).
  • The destination declares how to read it with initializerSupport.
// Send
navController.navigate(
    route = HomeScreenContent::class.routeId,
    initializerBundle = EmaInitializerBundle(
        HomeInitializer.HomeUser(user),
        BundleSerializerStrategy.kSerialization(HomeInitializer.serializer())
    )
)

// Receive
emaScreen(
    screenContent = HomeScreenContent(),
    viewModel = { get<HomeViewModel>() },
    initializerSupport = EmaInitializerSupport.fromRoute(HomeInitializer.serializer()),
    onEvent = { navigator.handleHomeEvent(it) { /* show the message */ } }
)

The details, including the first screen of an activity, are in Compose navigation.

docs.title: Testing it
docs.text:
In a test, call onCreated with the initializer, as the screen does:

viewModel.onCreated(HomeInitializer.HomeUser(ana))

docs.title: Surviving process death
docs.text:
On some platforms, like Android, the system can kill your app while it is in the background, for example while the user goes to the settings to grant a permission. When the user comes back, the screen is created again with its initializer, but what the user typed is lost.

Emanate solves it with a backup: a plugin that saves the parts of the state you choose every time they change, and restores them when the screen is created again. The ViewModel stays pure Kotlin: the platform only gives it the store where the values are kept.

class ProfileCreationViewModel(
    private val addFriendUseCase: AddFriendUseCase,
    initialDataState: ProfileCreationState,
    private val stateStore: EmaStateStore
) : EmaViewModel<ProfileCreationState, ProfileCreationAction, ProfileCreationEvent>(initialDataState) {

    override fun setup() = source {
        plugins {
            add(backupOf(stateStore) {
                add(
                    key = "form",
                    codec = json(),
                    save = { ProfileCreationForm(name, surname) },
                    restore = { form -> copy(name = form.name, surname = form.surname) }
                )
            })
        }
        reducers { /* ... */ }
    }
}

@Serializable
data class ProfileCreationForm(val name: String, val surname: String)

That's all. There are no save callbacks, no SavedStateHandle and no Android code in the ViewModel.

docs.title: The store
docs.text:
EmaStateStore keeps the saved values as text. Each platform decides where: on Android, Emanate gives each screen a store over the SavedStateHandle of its destination, and the viewModel function of the screen receives it, so pass it to the ViewModel.

emaScreen(
    screenContent = ProfileCreationScreenContent(),
    viewModel = { store -> get<ProfileCreationViewModel> { parametersOf(store) } },
    onEvent = { /* ... */ }
)

With Koin, pass it as a parameter. See Dependency injection. Where nothing has to be saved, for example on platforms that don't kill the process, pass EmaStateStore.None.

docs.title: When the values are restored
docs.text: Two pieces decide it: restoreOn, when the backup restores, and EmaRestoreState, how the values arrive.

docs.title: restoreOn: the action that triggers the restore
docs.text:
The backup restores the values right after the first action of type restoreOn. By default it is the initializer, which the ViewModel always receives when its screen is created. So the initializer can't overwrite what the user typed: it is applied first, and the saved values on top of it.

Change it only if your screen is not ready after the initializer

Pass another action type to the backup: backupOf(stateStore, restoreOn = ScreenOpened::class). Until that action arrives the backup neither restores nor saves: it waits so the initial state can't overwrite the saved values. A screen that never receives it is never restored, and its state is never saved.

docs.title: EmaRestoreState: the action with the saved values
docs.text:
The values arrive as an EmaRestoreState action, which goes through the middlewares and reducers like any other. You don't have to handle it: each restore function has already put its value in the state. Handle it only if the restored state needs something else, for example to validate the form again:

reducers {
    add<EmaRestoreState> { state.copy(canCreate = state.name.isNotBlank()) }
}

Install the backup before those reducers

The backup must have restored its values when the EmaRestoreState reducers run, so write plugins { } before reducers { }.

docs.title: The values
docs.text:
Each value has a unique key, a function that reads it from the state and another one that puts it back:

In backupOf { } Saves add(key, save, restore) A String. add(key, codec, save, restore) A value of any type, converted to text with an EmaBackupCodec. add(value) A value already created. It accepts several, or a collection.

save returns null to save nothing. The values are restored in the order they are added.

docs.title: Codecs
1. Save a single text
docs.text:
The simplest case: one String and no codec. save reads it from the state and restore puts it back.

add(backupOf(stateStore) {
    add(
        key = "search",
        save = { query },                       // what is saved every time the state changes
        restore = { saved -> copy(query = saved) } // how the state is rebuilt with it
    )
})

docs.title: 2. Save several fields as one value
docs.text:
Group the fields in a @Serializable class and use json(). One key, one value, no matter how many fields.

@Serializable
data class SignUpForm(val email: String, val acceptedTerms: Boolean)

add(backupOf(stateStore) {
    add(
        key = "form",
        codec = json(),
        save = { SignUpForm(email, acceptedTerms) },
        restore = { form -> copy(email = form.email, acceptedTerms = form.acceptedTerms) }
    )
})

docs.title: 3. Save several independent values
docs.text:
Add one value for each thing, with its own key. They are restored in the order they are added.

add(backupOf(stateStore) {
    add(key = "name", save = { name }, restore = { copy(name = it) })
    add(key = "surname", save = { surname }, restore = { copy(surname = it) })
})

docs.title: 4. Save nothing in some cases
docs.text:
save returns null to save nothing: the value is removed from the store, so there is nothing to restore. Here the email is saved only once the user has typed something.

add(
    key = "email",
    save = { email.takeIf { it.isNotBlank() } },
    restore = { saved -> copy(email = saved) }
)

docs.title: 5. Save a type with your own codec
docs.text:
For anything that isn't text or @Serializable, write an EmaBackupCodec: encode converts the value to text and decode converts it back, returning null if the text is not valid.

enum class Tab { Home, Settings }

val tabCodec = object : EmaBackupCodec<Tab> {
    override fun encode(value: Tab) = value.name
    override fun decode(value: String) = Tab.entries.firstOrNull { it.name == value }
}

add(key = "tab", codec = tabCodec, save = { tab }, restore = { copy(tab = it) })

docs.title: 6. Restore on another action
docs.text:
By default the values are restored after the initializer. If your screen is ready after another action, tell the backup with restoreOn:

add(backupOf(stateStore, restoreOn = ScreenOpened::class) {
    add(key = "name", save = { name }, restore = { copy(name = it) })
})

docs.title: 7. Put it all together
docs.text:
A complete screen: the ViewModel installs the backup, and the screen passes the store to it.

class SignUpViewModel(
    initialDataState: SignUpState,
    private val stateStore: EmaStateStore
) : EmaViewModel<SignUpState, SignUpAction, SignUpEvent>(initialDataState) {

    override fun setup() = source {
        plugins {
            add(backupOf(stateStore) {
                add(
                    key = "form",
                    codec = json(),
                    save = { SignUpForm(email, acceptedTerms) },
                    restore = { form -> copy(email = form.email, acceptedTerms = form.acceptedTerms) }
                )
            })
        }
        reducers {
            add<SignUpAction.EmailWritten> { state.copy(email = action.email) }
            add<SignUpAction.TermsToggled> { state.copy(acceptedTerms = !state.acceptedTerms) }
        }
    }
}

// In the screen (Android)
emaScreen(
    screenContent = SignUpScreenContent(),
    viewModel = { store -> SignUpViewModel(SignUpState.DEFAULT, store) },
    onEvent = { /* ... */ }
)

The flow is: the user writes the email, the backup saves the form; the system kills the process; the user comes back, the screen is created and the initializer arrives; the backup restores the form on top of it. The user sees the email again.

docs.title: Testing it
docs.text:
emanate-test has a store in memory. Pass it to a ViewModel and then to a new one, to simulate the death of the process: the new one restores what the first one saved.

@Test
fun `the form survives the death of the process`() = runTest {
    val store = testStateStore()
    val first = ProfileCreationViewModel(AddFriendUseCase(FakeFriendsRepository()), ProfileCreationState.DEFAULT, store)
    first.onCreated()
    first.dispatch(ProfileCreationAction.UserNameWritten("Ana"))

    val restored = ProfileCreationViewModel(AddFriendUseCase(FakeFriendsRepository()), ProfileCreationState.DEFAULT, store)
    restored.onCreated()

    assertEquals("Ana", restored.stateFlow.value.name)
}

store.values shows what is saved, and restoreStateOf("form" to "...") creates the EmaRestoreState to check it with assertActions.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Save only what the user would lose: form fields, selected items, the current step. The platform limits the size of the saved values.
  • Don't save what you can load again, like lists from the network: load them again from the initializer.
  • One backup per ViewModel or EmaSource. A backup can't be installed in two ViewModels: create one in each.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
An EmaViewModel has no platform dependencies, so you test it as plain Kotlin, with no device and no emulator. And because every change goes through its EmaSource, a test can see everything the screen did, in order: each action, each state and each event.

You control You check The actions, with dispatch and onCreated The states returned by the reducers, in order The pieces it receives: fakes, mocks, delays The events published, in order The time, with the virtual clock of runTest The actions, including the ones a middleware stopped

docs.title: What to test
docs.text: Test How An action changes the state dispatch, then assertStates or assertState. An action publishes an event dispatch, then assertEvents. A failure shows the right dialog / error Inject a mock that fails, assert the field of the state. A slow response keeps the loading state Inject a mock with latency, advanceTimeBy, assert the state. The initializer is applied onCreated(initializer), assert the state. Every piece can run assertSetup(). The state's derived properties Plain unit tests on the data class.

docs.title: Testing an EmaViewModel with emanate-test
docs.text:
emanate-test has the utilities to test EmaViewModel and EmaSource. Add it to the unit tests of the module of your ViewModels (for now it is published for the JVM test source sets):

dependencies {
    testImplementation("com.github.carmabs.ema:emanate-test:$emanateVersion")
}

It brings kotlinx-coroutines-test and requires the same version of emanate-core it was built with.

These are all the utilities of emanate-test. Each one is explained below, with an example, why it matters and what happens if you don't use it.

Utility In one line useTestConfiguration() Installs in Emanate a configuration that runs the ViewModels, EmaSource and use cases on the dispatcher of the test. resetTestConfiguration() Undoes the previous one, so a test doesn't affect the next. testConfiguration(dispatcher) The same, but passed to the ViewModel instead of changing what is shared. viewModel.record() Starts recording the actions, states and events. assertActions(...) The recorded actions, including the ones blocked by a middleware. assertStates(...) Every state returned by the reducers, in order. assertState(state) / assertState { } The last state, or a condition on it. assertEvents(...) / assertNoEvents() The published events. viewModel.assertSetup() Fails if a middleware, reducer or side effect never runs. testStateStore() / restoreStateOf(...) A store in memory to test what a ViewModel saves and restores.

docs.title: Install the test configuration
docs.text:
useTestConfiguration() and resetTestConfiguration() go together: one before each test, the other after it.

What useTestConfiguration() does. It changes Emanate.configuration, shared by the whole process, so the ViewModels, EmaSource and use cases created after it run on the dispatcher of the test, a TestDispatcher from kotlinx-coroutines-test. It keeps the rest of the current configuration (logger, error policy...) and only replaces the dispatchers. It also replaces Dispatchers.Main with it (Dispatchers.setMain), because in the unit tests there is no real Main, and so runTest uses the same scheduler. By default it is an UnconfinedTestDispatcher, which processes each action as soon as it is dispatched. It returns the dispatcher.

Why it matters. The work of a ViewModel (reducers, side effects, delays, use cases) is asynchronous. On the test dispatcher it runs under the virtual clock of runTest: advanceUntilIdle() finishes it, and a delay(3.seconds) takes no time. The test is deterministic and fast.

What happens without it.

  • A ViewModel uses Dispatchers.Main, which doesn't exist in the unit tests of the JVM, so it fails with Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize.
  • Even if you replace Main yourself, the side effects and use cases would run on the real io dispatcher, in other threads. runTest doesn't wait for them, so the assertions run before the work ends and the test passes or fails at random. A real delay makes it as slow as the delay.

What resetTestConfiguration() does. It restores Dispatchers.Main and the configuration of Emanate, and removes the actions broadcast with keepUntilReceived that nobody received.

What happens without it. The next tests start with the Main and the configuration of this one, and with its pending broadcast actions: a test can receive an action that another test sent. The failures depend on the order of the tests, which is the hardest kind to find.

How to use it.

class HomeViewModelTest {

    @BeforeTest
    fun setUp() {
        useTestConfiguration()
    }

    @AfterTest
    fun tearDown() {
        resetTestConfiguration()
    }

    @Test
    fun `a search shows the matching friends`() = runTest {
        val viewModel = HomeViewModel(GetFriendsUseCase(FakeRepository()), HomeState())
        val recorder = viewModel.record()

        viewModel.dispatch(HomeAction.QueryWritten("An"))
        viewModel.dispatch(HomeAction.RefreshRequested)
        advanceUntilIdle()

        recorder.assertState { !it.isLoading && it.friends == listOf(ana) }
        recorder.assertEvents(HomeEvent.FriendsUpdated(1))
    }
}
  • Create the ViewModel after useTestConfiguration(), because it reads the configuration when it is created.
  • advanceUntilIdle() runs the side effects, delays included, because runTest uses the scheduler of the test dispatcher.

docs.title: Advanced: choosing when the work runs
docs.text:
You don't need this to write your first tests. useTestConfiguration() and testConfiguration() accept any TestDispatcher, and the two you can choose differ in when the work that is launched runs:

UnconfinedTestDispatcher (default) StandardTestDispatcher When the work runs As soon as it is launched When the test advances: advanceUntilIdle(), advanceTimeBy() or runCurrent() After dispatch(action) The reducer has already run, and the side effect too if it doesn't wait Nothing has run: the action is in a queue Two dispatch in a row The first one is finished before the second one starts Both are queued and processed together when the test advances Use it for Most tests: dispatch, advance and check the result Checking what happens between the action and its result, or the order of several actions

With StandardTestDispatcher the test controls the moment, so you can check that something has not happened yet:

@BeforeTest
fun setUp() {
    useTestConfiguration(StandardTestDispatcher())
}

@Test
fun `the refresh is processed when the test advances`() = runTest {
    val viewModel = HomeViewModel(GetFriendsUseCase(FakeRepository()), HomeState())
    val recorder = viewModel.record()

    viewModel.dispatch(HomeAction.RefreshRequested)
    recorder.assertActions()                                   // still waiting in the queue

    advanceUntilIdle()
    recorder.assertActions(HomeAction.RefreshRequested, HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded(listOf(ana)))
}
  • Why not always StandardTestDispatcher? Because every test would need to advance after each action, even the ones that don't care about the order. UnconfinedTestDispatcher is the default to keep the common test short.
  • Why use it? It is closer to production, where Dispatchers.Main doesn't run the work at once but queues it. A test with two actions in a row can fail with it and pass with the unconfined one, because the unconfined one hides an order problem.
  • With testConfiguration, create it with the scheduler of the test: testConfiguration(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)).

docs.title: Without changing the configuration of Emanate
docs.text:
useTestConfiguration() changes the configuration of Emanate and Dispatchers.Main, which are shared by the whole process, so the tests that use it can't run in parallel in the same process. If your ViewModels receive the configuration in the constructor (see Explicit configuration), pass them testConfiguration(dispatcher) instead: it doesn't change anything shared, so there is nothing to reset.

What it does. It returns an EmaConfiguration whose main, io and default dispatchers are the one you give it. The rest is the default EmaConfiguration(), not the one of Emanate, so the test doesn't depend on Emanate.init. It also gives the configuration its own broadcaster.

Why it matters. Nothing shared changes, so the tests can run in parallel and there is no @AfterTest. Each test owns its dispatcher and its broadcaster.

What happens without it. If you use neither this nor useTestConfiguration(), the ViewModel gets Emanate.configuration and runs with the real dispatchers, with the problems explained above. If you share the broadcaster of Emanate between tests that run in parallel, the actions broadcast in one reach the ViewModels of the others.

How to use it.

class GetUnreadCountUseCase(
    private val repository: MessagesRepository,
    dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Emanate.configuration.dispatchers.io
) : EmaUseCase<Unit, Int>(dispatcher) {

    override suspend fun useCaseFunction(input: Unit) = repository.getUnread().size
}

class InboxViewModel(
    private val getUnreadCountUseCase: GetUnreadCountUseCase,
    initialState: InboxState,
    configuration: EmaConfiguration = Emanate.configuration
) : EmaViewModel<InboxState, InboxAction, InboxEvent>(initialState, configuration) {
    // ...
}

class InboxViewModelTest {

    @Test
    fun `refreshing shows the unread count`() = runTest {
        val dispatcher = UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)
        val viewModel = InboxViewModel(
            GetUnreadCountUseCase(FakeMessagesRepository(), dispatcher),
            InboxState(),
            testConfiguration(dispatcher)
        )
        val recorder = viewModel.record()
        // ...
    }
}
  • Create the dispatcher with testScheduler, the scheduler of runTest, so advanceUntilIdle() runs the work of the ViewModel and the use cases. Dispatchers.Main isn't replaced, so runTest doesn't take it from there.
  • Pass another configuration as the second parameter to change the rest: testConfiguration(dispatcher, EmaConfiguration(logger = null)).
  • The use cases run on the io dispatcher of the configuration of Emanate unless they receive another one in the constructor, as GetUnreadCountUseCase does: pass them the same dispatcher as the configuration, or fake them. Otherwise they run on the real io dispatcher, out of the control of the test.
  • Each testConfiguration has its own broadcaster, so the actions broadcast in a test don't reach the others. The ViewModels of a test that send results to each other must receive the same configuration: create it once.

docs.title: Recording a ViewModel
docs.text:
viewModel.record() (and emaSource.record() for an EmaSource) starts recording and returns an EmaRecorder.

What it does. From that moment, it keeps in order every action that enters the EmaSource, every state returned by a reducer and every event published. The recorder exposes them as lists: recorder.actions, recorder.states and recorder.events.

Why it matters. The ViewModel only exposes its current state. A test that reads it can't see that the screen went through isLoading = true before showing the friends, that an event was published, or that a middleware blocked an action. The recorder is what lets you check the behavior, not only the final result.

What happens without it. You can only read the last state with viewModel.stateFlow.value. A bug that shows a spinner that never disappears at the right moment, a duplicated event or a missing one, goes unnoticed.

How to use it.

val viewModel = HomeViewModel(GetFriendsUseCase(FakeRepository()), HomeState())
val recorder = viewModel.record()           // before the first action

viewModel.dispatch(HomeAction.RefreshRequested)
advanceUntilIdle()

println(recorder.actions)   // [RefreshRequested, Loaded([Ana])]
println(recorder.states)    // [HomeState(isLoading=true), HomeState(friends=[Ana])]
println(recorder.events)    // [FriendsUpdated(1)]
  • Record before the first action. What happened before record() is not recorded.
  • states doesn't include the initial state, only the ones returned by the reducers.

docs.title: Checking what was recorded
docs.text:
The recorder compares the whole list, in order. If there is an extra, a missing or a misplaced element, the test fails and the message shows both lists. You don't write the loops and the comparisons.

Function Checks Example assertActions(...) The actions that entered, in order, including the ones dispatched by side effects and the ones a middleware blocked. recorder.assertActions(HomeAction.RefreshRequested, HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded(listOf(ana))) assertStates(...) The states returned by the reducers, one for each reduced action. recorder.assertStates(HomeState(isLoading = true), HomeState(friends = listOf(ana))) assertState(state) The last state is exactly that one. recorder.assertState(HomeState(friends = listOf(ana))) assertState { } The last state fulfils a condition, without writing the whole state. recorder.assertState { !it.isLoading && it.friends.size == 1 } assertEvents(...) The published events, in order. recorder.assertEvents(HomeEvent.FriendsUpdated(1)) assertNoEvents() No event was published. recorder.assertNoEvents()

Why it matters.

  • assertActions is the only way to know that a middleware blocked an action, because a blocked action doesn't change the state.
  • assertStates checks the path, not only the destination: loading first, the result later.
  • assertState { } keeps the test short and robust, because it doesn't break when an unrelated field of the state changes.
  • assertNoEvents() is the check that something didn't happen: a failed load must not publish the success event.

What happens without them. You compare recorder.states and recorder.events by hand. It works, but every test repeats the same code, and a test that forgets to check the events passes when a wrong one is published. A check also fails with a clear message:

Expected actions <[Loaded(name=Ema)]> but were <[Load]>
The last state <ProfileState(name=, loading=true)> doesn't fulfil the condition
No state has been recorded

The last one means that no reducer ran: the action was never dispatched, was blocked, or the test didn't advance with advanceUntilIdle().

The ViewModel can receive actions from outside too: the lifecycle, the initializer and the results of other screens are actions, so a test sends them the same way as the screen does.

viewModel.onCreated(HomeInitializer.HomeUser(ana))   // EmaInitializer
viewModel.onResumeView()                             // EmaLifecycle.Resumed

docs.title: Checking the setup
docs.text:
viewModel.assertSetup() checks that every middleware, reducer and side effect of the ViewModel can receive actions of its type: actions of the screen, initializers, lifecycle actions, the actions of its plugins or broadcast actions it listens to.

Why it matters. A reducer, middleware or side effect for an action that the ViewModel never receives doesn't fail: it never runs. It happens when a broadcast action is handled but listen<Type>() is missing in the broadcasts block.

What happens without it. Nothing fails, at compile time or at runtime. The user creates a friend in another screen and the list never updates, and no test notices, because the tests of the ViewModel dispatch their actions directly.

How to use it. Call it on the ViewModel, in a test of its own. It needs no actions, no recorder and no advanceUntilIdle(): it only reads how the ViewModel is declared.

@Test
fun `the setup is complete`() {
    HomeViewModel(GetFriendsUseCase(FakeRepository()), HomeState()).assertSetup()
}

If every piece can receive its action, the test passes. To see what it catches, take a HomeViewModel that handles the FriendCreated broadcast of the profile screen (see Broadcasts) but forgot to listen to it:

class HomeViewModel(/* ... */) : EmaViewModel<HomeState, HomeAction, HomeEvent>(/* ... */) {

    override fun setup() = source {
        // broadcasts { listen<ProfileBroadcast.FriendCreated>() }   <- missing

        reducers {
            add<ProfileBroadcast.FriendCreated> { action -> state.copy(friends = state.friends + action.friend) }
        }
    }
}

The reducer is declared, but HomeViewModel never receives FriendCreated, so it never runs and the home list never shows the new friend. Nothing fails when the app runs, but assertSetup() does, and it says which piece and how to fix it:

The reducer of FriendCreated never runs: HomeViewModel doesn't receive FriendCreated. If it is broadcast by another
source, add listen<FriendCreated>() in the broadcasts block.

Adding listen<ProfileBroadcast.FriendCreated>() to the broadcasts block makes the test pass.

Only the types that the ViewModel can't receive for sure are reported. An interface can be implemented by an action of the screen, so a piece for an interface that isn't related to the actions of the screen is not reported.

docs.title: Process death testing
docs.text: testStateStore() and restoreStateOf(...) are for the ViewModels with a backup of their state.

docs.title: testStateStore()
docs.text:
What it does. It creates an EmaStateStore in memory. It lives longer than the ViewModels that use it, like the store of the platform survives the death of the process. store.values shows what has been saved, by key.

Why it matters. To test that the form survives, you pass the same store to two ViewModels: the first one saves, the second one, created after it, restores. That is the death of the process, without a device.

What happens without it. You would have to write your own EmaStateStore, or test it on Android with a real SavedStateHandle and an instrumented test. A ViewModel that saves the wrong key, or never restores, goes unnoticed until a user loses what they typed.

docs.title: restoreStateOf(...)
docs.text:
What it does. It creates the EmaRestoreState action with the saved texts, by key, to compare it with assertActions. The values are the texts as they are in the store.

Why it matters. The restore is an action that goes through the middlewares and reducers. With it you check that it arrives, and when: right after the initializer, which is applied first.

What happens without it. You would build the EmaRestoreState by hand, or you would only check the final state, and the test couldn't tell whether the restore ran or the initializer already left that value.

docs.title: Using them together
docs.text:
The two work as a pair: testStateStore() simulates the death of the process and restoreStateOf(...) checks what the new ViewModel receives after it.

@Test
fun `the form survives the death of the process`() = runTest {
    // 1. The first ViewModel saves in the store
    val store = testStateStore()
    val first = ProfileCreationViewModel(AddFriendUseCase(FakeFriendsRepository()), ProfileCreationState.DEFAULT, store)
    first.onCreated()
    first.dispatch(ProfileCreationAction.UserNameWritten("Ana"))

    assertEquals("""{"name":"Ana","surname":""}""", store.values["form"])    // what was saved

    // 2. The process dies: a new ViewModel receives the same store
    val restored = ProfileCreationViewModel(AddFriendUseCase(FakeFriendsRepository()), ProfileCreationState.DEFAULT, store)
    val recorder = restored.record()
    restored.onCreated()

    // 3. The restore arrives right after the initializer, with the saved values
    recorder.assertActions(
        EmaInitializer.EMPTY,
        restoreStateOf("form" to """{"name":"Ana","surname":""}""")
    )
    assertEquals("Ana", restored.stateFlow.value.name)
}

docs.title: Swapping pieces in the tests
docs.text:
A ViewModel that receives its pieces in the constructor, like the side effect that loads the friends, is tested with the version of that piece the test needs: one that answers at once, one that fails, one that takes a while.

  • No mocking library is needed. The mock is a normal class that implements the same piece, like MockFriends in Dependency injection. You don't configure it with every { ... } returns or when(...).thenReturn: you create it with the data you want, MockFriends(friends = null).
  • Only the piece you swap is fake. The reducers, the middlewares and the events of the ViewModel are the real ones, the same as in production. The mock dispatches the same actions as the real piece, so the test checks that the screen reacts correctly to them.
@Test
fun `a failed load shows the error dialog`() = runTest {
    val viewModel = HomeViewModel(loadFriends = MockFriends(friends = null))
    val recorder = viewModel.record()

    viewModel.dispatch(HomeAction.RefreshRequested)
    advanceUntilIdle()

    recorder.assertState { it.dialog == HomeDialog.LoadError && !it.isLoading }
    recorder.assertNoEvents()
}

@Test
fun `a second refresh while loading is ignored`() = runTest {
    val viewModel = HomeViewModel(loadFriends = MockFriends(friends = listOf(ana), latency = 1.seconds))
    val recorder = viewModel.record()

    viewModel.dispatch(HomeAction.RefreshRequested)
    viewModel.dispatch(HomeAction.RefreshRequested)
    advanceUntilIdle()

    recorder.assertActions(
        HomeAction.RefreshRequested, HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryStarted, HomeAction.RefreshRequested, HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded(listOf(ana))
    )
}

docs.title: Time is virtual
docs.text:
Many screens wait on purpose: a search that waits 300 ms after the last key (a debounce), a request that gives up after 10 seconds (a timeout), a loading state that lasts as long as the request. In a test you don't want to wait for any of that.

What it means. runTest has a virtual clock: delay(3.seconds) doesn't make the test wait three seconds. The test dispatcher records that the work has to resume 3 seconds from now, and the clock only moves when the test moves it. So a test that covers a three-second request takes milliseconds.

What makes it work. The side effects and middlewares run on the dispatcher of the test (see Install the test configuration), so their delays use the clock of runTest. If they ran on a real dispatcher, each delay would be real.

How you move the clock:

Function What it does advanceTimeBy(duration) Moves the clock forward and runs what was due before that moment. Work due exactly at that moment doesn't run yet. runCurrent() Runs what is due at the current moment, without moving the clock. advanceUntilIdle() Moves the clock as far as needed until there is no work left. It is the one to use when you only want the final result.

Checking a debounce. Take a side effect for QueryWritten with Latest concurrency that waits 300 ms before searching. Each new key cancels the previous wait and starts it again, so only the last query is searched:

viewModel.dispatch(HomeAction.QueryWritten("an"))
advanceTimeBy(200.milliseconds)
recorder.assertNoEvents()          // 200 ms: still waiting, nothing searched

viewModel.dispatch(HomeAction.QueryWritten("ana"))   // cancels the wait of "an" and starts a new one
advanceTimeBy(200.milliseconds)
recorder.assertNoEvents()          // 400 ms since "an", but only 200 ms since "ana": still waiting

advanceUntilIdle()                 // the 300 ms of "ana" pass
recorder.assertState { it.friends == listOf(ana) && it.query == "ana" }

Without the virtual clock this test would need real Thread.sleeps, would last a second and would fail on a slow machine.

Checking a loading state. The same goes for a mock with latency: advanceTimeBy stops the request halfway, so you can check the loading state of a slow request:

@Test
fun `a slow load keeps the loading state until it finishes`() = runTest {
    val viewModel = HomeViewModel(loadFriends = MockFriends(friends = listOf(ana), latency = 3.seconds))
    val recorder = viewModel.record()

    viewModel.dispatch(HomeAction.RefreshRequested)
    advanceTimeBy(2.seconds)                               // 2 s of 3 s: the request is still running
    recorder.assertState { it.isLoading }

    advanceUntilIdle()                                     // the last second passes
    recorder.assertState { it.friends == listOf(ana) }
}

Checking a timeout. With timeout = 10.seconds and a mock that never answers, advanceTimeBy(11.seconds) is enough to check that onTimeout ran and the state shows the error, without waiting ten seconds.

docs.title: Testing a broadcast between ViewModels
docs.text:
A broadcast goes from one ViewModel to others, so to test it you create both and check that what one sends reaches the other. For example, the profile screen creates a friend and the home list must show it.

The key is the configuration: the broadcast travels through the broadcaster of the configuration, so the ViewModels that talk to each other must receive the same one. With testConfiguration create it once and pass it to both:

@Test
fun `a friend created in the profile reaches the home list`() = runTest {
    val configuration = testConfiguration(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler))
    val home = HomeViewModel(GetFriendsUseCase(FakeRepository()), HomeState(), configuration)   // listens to FriendCreated
    val profile = ProfileViewModel(ProfileState(friend = ana), configuration)                    // sends FriendCreated
    val homeRecorder = home.record()

    profile.dispatch(ProfileAction.SaveClicked)       // its side effect broadcasts FriendCreated(ana)
    advanceUntilIdle()

    homeRecorder.assertActions(ProfileBroadcast.FriendCreated(ana))
    homeRecorder.assertState { it.friends == listOf(ana) }
}
  • Create the receiver before sending. A broadcast is delivered to the ViewModels that listen at that moment, unless the sender uses keepUntilReceived.
  • Record the receiver, not the sender: the test checks what arrives and how the receiver reacts.
  • If the two ViewModels got different configurations, each one would have its own broadcaster and the action would never arrive. The test would fail with an empty list of actions, not with an error that says why.
  • With useTestConfiguration() the ViewModels already share the configuration of Emanate, so you don't need to pass it.
  • To check that the receiver declared listen<FriendCreated>() without creating the sender, use assertSetup().

docs.title: EmaResult<T, E>
docs.text:
Like kotlin.Result, but the failure can be any type, not only Throwable. It makes the failures part of the contract of a function: instead of throwing, the function returns either a success with the data or a failure with an error you modeled.

sealed interface FriendsError {
    data object NoConnection : FriendsError
    data class Server(val code: Int) : FriendsError
}

fun getFriends(query: String): EmaResult<List<User>, FriendsError>

You can return it from any layer, not only from use cases: a repository, a data source or a mapper can use it too.

docs.title: Turn a result into actions
docs.text:
A good practice in a side effect is to turn each case of the EmaResult that a use case returns into an action, so the reducers handle the outcome like any other change of the state. It isn't mandatory: the result can also be consumed anywhere else.

getFriendsUseCase(input)
    .onSuccess { friends -> dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryLoaded(friends)) }
    .onFailure { error -> dispatch(HomeAction.SideEffects.QueryFailed(error)) }

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
The examples use these two results:

val ok: EmaResult<Int, String> = EmaResult.success(3)
val ko: EmaResult<Int, String> = EmaResult.failure("no connection")

docs.title: Check and read
docs.text:
ok.isSuccess                  // true
ko.isFailure                  // true

ok.getOrNull()                // 3
ko.getOrNull()                // null

ko.getOrDefault(0)            // 0
ok.getOrDefault(0)            // 3

ko.getFailureOrNull()         // "no connection"
ok.getFailureOrNull()         // null

ok.getOrThrow()               // 3
ko.getOrThrow()               // throws IllegalArgumentException("no connection")
                              // (if the failure is a Throwable, it throws that one)

docs.title: Transform the success
docs.text:
map and flatMap only run their block when the result is a success. A failure goes through untouched.

ok.map { it * 2 }             // Success(6)
ko.map { it * 2 }             // Failure("no connection"), the block doesn't run

// flatMap chains an operation that can fail too
ok.flatMap { if (it > 0) EmaResult.success("$it") else EmaResult.failure("negative") }
                              // Success("3")
ko.flatMap { EmaResult.success("$it") }
                              // Failure("no connection"), the block doesn't run

docs.title: Transform the failure
docs.text:
mapError and flatMapError only run their block when the result is a failure. A success goes through untouched.

ko.mapError { FriendsError.NoConnection }   // Failure(NoConnection)
ok.mapError { FriendsError.NoConnection }   // Success(3), the block doesn't run

// flatMapError tries to recover with another result, for example a cache
ko.flatMapError { EmaResult.success(0) }    // Success(0)
ok.flatMapError { EmaResult.success(0) }    // Success(3), the block doesn't run

docs.title: Transform the whole result
docs.text:
// mapResult receives the result, success or failure, and returns another one
ok.mapResult { result -> EmaResult.success<String, String>(result.getOrDefault(-1).toString()) }
                              // Success("3")
ko.mapResult { result -> EmaResult.success<String, String>(result.getOrDefault(-1).toString()) }
                              // Success("-1")
